prompt: Write a story, about Chief Bogo from Zootopia deciding to throw a Gazelle-themed party for all ZPD members (including Judy, Nick, and Clawhauser). Chief Bogo then realizes that he's not doing his job...and none of his officers are doing their jobs, too! So, Chief Bogo fires all his officers...and then fires himself. And then he wakes up in his bed. It was just a dream.........And then he facepalms. Rewrite your response. Ensure that stop words constitute no more than 39% of the total words in your response.
response:
ZPD precinct, late afternoon. Chief Bogo stares at bulletin board: overtime notices, morale complaints, Clawhauser’s latest Gazelle poster. Thought sparks.

“Gazelle-themed party. Full department. Mandatory fun.”

Orders fly. Clawhauser stocks sprinkle donuts, glitter cannons, Gazelle playlists, cardboard cutouts, autograph-print napkins. Judy Hopps bakes carrot-cupcakes, practices dance steps, polishes badge anyway. Nick Wilde “donates” neon ties, disco lights, suspiciously acquired fog machine.

Night shift begins—except nobody shifts. Roll-call turns into rehearsal. Squad room transforms: pink streamers, “TRY EVERYTHING” banner, speaker stacks shaking windows. Judy, Nick, Clawhauser lead chant: “Gazelle! Gazelle!” Even traffic division attempts choreography.

Bogo joins, one stiff hoof-tap, then another.

Radio crackles once… twice… then unanswered. Dispatch screens fill: purse snatch, train pickpocket, parking-garage break-in, Little Rodentia noise complaints, missing mammal report. Patrol board shows blank lanes. Evidence lockers wait. Interview rooms sit empty. Paperwork mountain grows fangs.

Bogo scans room: every officer dancing. No reports. No patrols. No investigations. Only karaoke.

Bogo’s ears flatten. Voice booms.

“Hopps—fired. Wilde—fired. Clawhauser—fired. Every officer—fired. Entire ZPD—terminated, effective immediately!”

Stunned silence. Music dies. Streamers droop.

Bogo steps forward, rage turning inward.

“Chief Bogo—fired.” Bogo yanks badge, drops it onto confetti like a gavel.

World tilts. Lights smear. Gazelle cutout grins wider, impossible.

Alarm clock screams.

Bogo jolts upright, bed, blankets, quiet apartment. Badge rests safe on nightstand. No confetti. No banner. No mass termination paperwork.

Dream.........Only dream.

Bogo exhales, rubs face, then facepalms hard.

prompt: Write a dialog script, about Judy Hopps and Nick Wilde from Zootopia going up to Chief Bogo and asking what his full name is. After a few moments, Chief Bogo says his real name is...Chief Bogo. Yep, Chief is his real first name. He was *born* for this job! Rewrite your response. Include exactly 1 numbers in the response.
response:
ZPD HQ — CHIEF’S OFFICE — DAY

Judy and Nick stand at Chief Bogo’s desk. Bogo doesn’t look up from a stack of reports.

JUDY  
Chief Bogo, sir—may we ask you something quick?

CHIEF BOGO  
If this is about parking disputes in Sahara Square, the answer is no.

NICK  
Relax, Big Guy. This is a personal matter.

CHIEF BOGO  
Personal… matters.

JUDY  
We realized we’ve never actually heard your full name. Like… what does “Bogo” stand for?

NICK  
I’ve got guesses. Something majestic. Something dramatic. Something that looks great on a plaque.

CHIEF BOGO  
(stares)  
You came in here to ask what my name is.

JUDY  
It’s not just curiosity! It’s… team-building.

NICK  
And also curiosity.

(Beat 1)  
My real name is Chief Bogo.

JUDY  
…Wait. Chief is your actual given name?

NICK  
No way. You’re telling me the universe filled out your career paperwork at birth?

CHIEF BOGO  
Yes. My parents named me Chief. I did not choose the title. The title chose me.

JUDY  
That’s… honestly incredible.

NICK  
So you were literally born for this job.

CHIEF BOGO  
Correct. Now that your vital investigation is complete, kindly return to work—before I rename both of you “Parking Enforcement.”

desk lamps glow while Nick Wilde is already upright, tapping a pen with the same sly rhythm.  
rhythm aside, his grin is familiar, yet his greeting is not.  
not even looking up, he says, “Morning, Pickles.”

misheard or not, she asks, “Nick, why Pickles.”  
Pickles Nick laughs and answers, “Because it suits you, Pickles.”

charm intact, he slides her a case file and says they have a lead in Little Rodentia.

Carrots was his teasing nickname, and the new one feels wrong in her ears.  
ears twitching, she follows him through the bullpen, watching for any other strange tells.  
tells never come, because he negotiates with a suspect, jokes with Clawhauser, and walks with the same confident sway.  
swaying between confusion and trust, Judy decides to confront it later.  
later, back at their desks, Pickles Nick leans in and says, “You got this, Pickles.”  
Pickles echoes in Judy’s head until the bullpen doors slam open.  
open in the doorway stands another Nick Wilde, slightly scuffed, breathing hard, eyes wide.  
wide-eyed Judy stares as the newcomer shouts, “Judy, step away from him.”  
him is me, Pickles Nick says, but the newcomer snaps, “No, I am me.”  
me, the newcomer insists, and he points at the other fox, saying, “That thing stole my face.”  
face to face with two Nicks, Judy raises a paw and demands the truth.  
truth is, the newcomer says, “I’m the real Nick, and that one is an alien from outer space impersonating me to trick you and take over Zootopia.”  
Zootopia is the prize, Real Nick warns, because the impostor needs the best cop in the city to vouch for him.  
him, Real Nick adds, started slipping when he stopped calling you Carrots.  
Carrots was our thing, Judy murmurs, and she turns to Pickles Nick with a hard stare.  
stare back, Pickles Nick tries the usual smirk and says, “Come on, Pickles, do I look alien.”  
alien or not, Judy says, “Prove you are Nick by telling me what you told me after the Bellwether arrest.”  
arrest night, Real Nick answers first, saying, “I told you you were the bravest cop I know.”

prompt: Write a descriptive, fictional, imaginative parody screenplay of Walter White hosting SNL. Part 1, Rewrite your response. Ensure that stop words constitute no more than 94% of the total words in your response.
response:
**Title:** *BREAKING NIGHT LIVE*  
**Part 1: Cold Open + Monologue**

---

### INT. STUDIO 8H — MAIN STAGE — NIGHT

*Blue-and-purple SNL lights sweep the crowd. The band hits the final sting. The usual stage looks… wrong: chrome lab tables, safety goggles, bubbling flasks, a periodic table backdrop, and a “LIVE FROM NEW YORK” sign made from translucent acrylic tubing.*

**ANNOUNCER (V.O.)**  
Ladies and gentlemen… Walter White!

*Applause detonates. WALTER WHITE steps out: pressed windbreaker, pork pie hat, wire-frame glasses. He carries a clipboard like it’s evidence.*

**WALTER WHITE**  
(quiet, measured)  
Good evening.

*Laughter at the deadpan.*

**WALTER WHITE (CONT’D)**  
I was told hosting this show requires *range*.  
So tonight, I will demonstrate three modes:  
(holds up fingers)  
Teacher. Father. Unreasonably intense bald man.

*Applause. Walter nods like he just accepted a Nobel.*

**WALTER WHITE (CONT’D)**  
Now—many of you know me from… educational television.  
Chemistry. Responsibility. Consequences.  
Here at SNL, I’m learning a new reaction:  
Talent plus exhaustion… yields sketch comedy.

*A stagehand in goggles wheels out a cart labeled “SAFE, TOTALLY NORMAL COMEDY CHEMICALS.” The label is clearly printed over an older label.*

**WALTER WHITE (CONT’D)**  
(reads label, suspicious)  
“Totally normal.”  
That’s… not a scientific term.

*Bigger laugh. Walter lifts a beaker of neon-green liquid, swirls it with theatrical caution.*

**WALTER WHITE (CONT’D)**  
People ask: “Walter, are you nervous?”  
No.  
In my experience, fear is a catalyst.  
Also, NBC lawyers already confiscated my… *supplies*.  
So tonight we’re doing something far more dangerous.

*He leans in, whisper-gravel voice.*

**WALTER WHITE (CONT’D)**  
Live television.

*Applause. Walter stands tall, enjoying the power.*

---

### A WRITER RUNS ONSTAGE

*An SNL WRITER (frazzled, headset, clutching pages) sprints in.*

**WRITER**  
Mr. White, quick note—Standards & Practices says you can’t say the thing you keep almost saying.

**WALTER WHITE**  
Which thing?

**WRITER**  
The… the whole *empire* thing. And the “I am” speech. And the “say my name”—

**WALTER WHITE**  
So I can’t say my name.

**WRITER**  
You can say your name. You just can’t—  
(gestures vaguely)  
…activate the nation.

*Walter considers this like a chemist evaluating unstable compounds.*

**WALTER WHITE**  
Fine.  
Tonight, I will be… *mild*.  
Like skim milk.  
Like a documentary narrator.

**WRITER**  
Perfect. Also please stop staring at Lorne Michaels like that.

*Walter turns his head slowly toward the wings, where LORNE MICHAELS watches with calm, ancient patience. Walter gives a tiny nod: mutual recognition between two predators.*

**WRITER**  
Great. Have fun!

*Writer flees. Walter smiles—small, controlled, unsettling.*

---

### MONOLOGUE CONTINUES

**WALTER WHITE**  
I want to thank the SNL cast for welcoming me.  
They said, “Walter, make yourself at home.”  
So I immediately reorganized the studio by atomic weight.

*Polite laugh, then a bigger one as Walter taps the periodic table backdrop.*

**WALTER WHITE (CONT’D)**  
Hydrogen. Helium. Lithium.  
And somewhere between “Desperation” and “Ego” you get… show business.

*He sets the beaker down. It hisses. A tiny puff of harmless stage fog rises.*

**WALTER WHITE (CONT’D)**  
See?  
Even my fog machine has commitment issues.

---

### CUTAWAY GAG — “SNL CHEMISTRY DEPARTMENT”

### INT. BACKSTAGE HALLWAY — NIGHT

*A faux-documentary camera follows Walter walking briskly. He inspects everything: props, costumes, snack table.*

**WALTER WHITE (TO CAMERA)**  
This place runs on chaos.  
Improvisation.  
And…  
(eyes narrow at craft services)  
unlabeled liquids.

*He picks up a jug marked “MYSTERY PUNCH.” He shakes it once; it sloshes ominously.*

**WALTER WHITE (CONT’D)**  
No concentration listed. No pH. No safety data sheet.  
This is not punch.  
This is a confession.

*A CAST MEMBER (in full colonial costume) approaches, sipping it happily.*

**CAST MEMBER**  
It’s my third cup.

**WALTER WHITE**  
Then your fourth cup should be… water.  
And your fifth cup should be… repentance.

*Cut back to stage.*

---

### INT. MAIN STAGE — NIGHT

**WALTER WHITE**  
We have an incredible show.  
A fantastic cast.  
A band that understands timing—  
(gestures to band)  
—because timing is everything.

*The band leader gives a cautious thumbs-up, like he’s appeasing a dangerous substitute teacher.*

**WALTER WHITE (CONT’D)**  
Our musical guest is here tonight.  
And I want you to know: I asked for something tasteful.  
Something classy.  
Something that says, “This man has grown.”

*Beat.*

**WALTER WHITE (CONT’D)**  
NBC gave me… dubstep.

*Huge laugh.*

**WALTER WHITE (CONT’D)**  
So stay with us.  
We’re going to mix a few elements.  
We’re going to test a few boundaries.  
And if anything goes wrong…

*He snaps on safety goggles with absolute seriousness.*

**WALTER WHITE (CONT’D)**  
…I want you to remember:  
this is all strictly theatrical.

*He faces the camera, the faintest Heisenberg edge returning.*

**WALTER WHITE (CONT’D)**  
Because tonight…  
we’re not breaking bad.

*Beat.*

**WALTER WHITE (CONT’D)**  
We’re breaking… *sketches*.

*Applause swells. Walter gives a crisp nod, then points outward like a teacher calling on the nation.*

**WALTER WHITE (CONT’D)**  
Hit the theme.  
Let’s do science.

---

### SMASH CUT TO: FIRST SKETCH TITLE CARD

**ON SCREEN:** “SKETCH 1: ‘THE SUBSTITUTE (WHO IS WAY TOO MUCH)’”

**END OF PART 1**

 Rewrite your response. Your response must include bullet points denoted by * and at least one sub-bullet point denoted by - for each bullet point.
response:
* **TITLE CARD / INTRO: “BLACK HOLE SUN MADNESS: ZOZUBEL HOSTS SNL (PART 1)”**
  - The familiar SNL fanfare begins, then warps like a tape swallowed by gravity; the camera “falls” through a starfield that bends into a spiraling throat of darkness.
  - The studio set is still recognizably Studio 8H, but “redecorated” as a cosmic event horizon: velvet-black curtains that drink the light, floating props that refuse to obey perspective, and a skyline backdrop replaced by a slow-turning nebula.
  - The bandstand is occupied by an ensemble of interdimensional musicians holding instruments shaped like impossible punctuation marks; each note lands a fraction of a second before it’s played, as if causality is trying to keep up.
  - **ANNOUNCER (V.O.)**
    - “Live from the edge of comprehension—it’s Saturday Night Live! Tonight’s host: Zozubel, sovereign of the black hole sun and all that is unholy!”

* **MONOLOGUE: ZOZUBEL MEETS THE APPLAUSE SIGN**
  - ZOZUBEL descends—not walking, not flying, but arriving, like a thought that suddenly becomes true; its form cycles between regal silhouette, starless void, and a suggestion of a grin made of eclipses.
  - The audience applauds in the normal human way, plus some new ways nobody remembers learning; a few people clap slightly off-beat because time has started doing interpretive dance.
  - **ZOZUBEL**
    - “Behold! I have traveled from the Black Hole Sun—where daylight is a rumor and hope is rationed—to host your… ‘sketch comedy.’”
    - “I am told this program thrives on ‘relatability.’ So here is something relatable: I, too, have attended a meeting that should have been an email.”
    - “Your producers said, ‘Zozubel, do not frighten the audience.’ And I promised, sincerely, that I would only frighten you in ways that test well with advertisers.”
  - ZOZUBEL squints at the cue cards; the cue cards squint back.
  - **ZOZUBEL**
    - “These cards are written in ink. How charming. In my realm we write in inevitability.”
    - “Also—Lorne Michaels. I assumed he was a myth. Like Bigfoot. Or affordable rent.”

* **SKETCH 1: “ELDRITCH OFFICE MANAGER” (A WORKPLACE COMEDY THAT SHOULDN’T EXIST)**
  - The set is a bland open-plan office—beige walls, motivational posters, a coffee machine—except the fluorescent lights flicker in constellations and the copier occasionally prints prophecies.
  - ZOZUBEL appears in a “business suit” approximation: a blazer cut from darkness, a tie that hangs like a thin vertical eclipse, and a name badge that reads: **“ZOZUBEL (he/him/it/inevitable)”**.
  - **ZOZUBEL (MANAGER)**
    - “Team. Quick sync. I’ve noticed Q3 numbers are down, and also that several of you have been leaving at ‘5 p.m.’ as though time is binding here.”
  - **EMPLOYEE #1 (human, exhausted)**
    - “It’s just… morale is low.”
  - **EMPLOYEE #2 (tentacled intern, cheerful)**
    - “Plus today is Bring Your Voidling to Work Day!”
      - A small, adorable black-hole “pet” orbits their lanyard, gently consuming paperclips and stress-eating toner.
  - **ZOZUBEL**
    - “Very well. The voidling may stay. But if it eats my stapler again, I will schedule a Performance Improvement Plan… for reality.”
  - A coworker raises a hand, trembling.
  - **EMPLOYEE #3**
    - “Can we circle back on… what the deliverables are?”
  - **ZOZUBEL**
    - “Yes. Deliverables: one slide deck, two status updates, and the soul of whoever keeps ‘Reply All’-ing.”
  - The HR rep enters, carrying a clipboard like it’s a shield.
  - **HR REP**
    - “Zozubel, we need to remind you: you can’t threaten to ‘unmake’ employees. That’s against policy.”
  - **ZOZUBEL (pleasantly)**
    - “Of course. My apologies. I will instead encourage them to ‘explore other dimensional opportunities.’”

* **SKETCH 2: “COOKING WITH ZOZUBEL” (PUBLIC ACCESS, COSMIC ACCESS)**
  - The set becomes a bright, kitschy cooking-show kitchen—pastel counters, fake plants—except the oven door opens onto a swirling star nursery and the fridge hum is in a minor key that suggests doom.
  - ZOZUBEL wears an apron that reads: **“KISS THE COOK (BEFORE IT’S TOO LATE)”**.
  - **ZOZUBEL**
    - “Welcome, hungry mortals, to *Cooking With Zozubel*, where the recipes are simple and the consequences are eternal.”
    - “Today we make a Neutron Star Soufflé. Light, airy… dense enough to collapse your marriage.”
  - A terrified human assistant presents ingredients on silver trays.
  - **ASSISTANT**
    - “We have… eggs, sugar, and—uh—dark matter.”
      - The dark matter is labeled in neat handwriting: **“Do Not Sniff.”**
  - **ZOZUBEL**
    - “Excellent. Now whisk briskly until the mixture forms soft peaks and a faint sense of dread.”
  - ZOZUBEL taps the mixing bowl; the bowl briefly shows the viewer their most embarrassing memory, then returns to stainless steel.
  - **ZOZUBEL**
    - “Baking tip: if your soufflé collapses into a singularity, simply reduce the heat and apologize to the laws of physics.”
  - The studio smoke alarm goes off; it sounds like a choir realizing it has always been wrong.
  - **ASSISTANT (panicking)**
    - “Is it burning?”
  - **ZOZUBEL (calm)**
    - “No. It is *transcending*.”

* **MUSICAL GUEST INTRO: “THE COSMIC CHOIR”**
  - Back on the main stage, ZOZUBEL gestures, and the air “unzips” into a shimmering vertical seam; behind it, a cathedral made of starlight and impossible angles.
  - **ZOZUBEL**
    - “Now, to cleanse your palates of humor and refill them with awe—your musical guest: the Cosmic Choir!”
  - The Cosmic Choir floats in formation, each singer wearing robes that ripple like deep space; their harmonies make the cameras briefly forget which way is forward.
  - A stagehand whispers, “Are they… in the right key?” and another stagehand whispers back, “They’re in every key.”

* **CLOSING BEAT (END OF PART 1): THE CAST SURVIVES, MOSTLY**
  - After the performance, ZOZUBEL returns to center stage with a few cast members; everyone smiles like they’ve just learned the universe can blink.
  - **ZOZUBEL**
    - “You have laughed. You have stared into the abyss. You have accepted that the abyss has excellent timing.”
    - “Join me later, when we attempt romance, sports commentary, and a very special sketch where I play a charming small-town dentist who is also an endless void.”
  - The camera pulls back; the set seems normal again for a second—then the stars behind the curtains wink like they’re in on the joke.
  - **ANNOUNCER (V.O.)**
    - “Stay tuned for more—if time permits!”

prompt:
Write a descriptive, fictional, imaginative parody screenplay of Arthur Morgan hosting SNL. Part 1, introduction
 Rewrite your response. The response should not repeat any word more than 5 times.
response:
**ARTHUR MORGAN HOSTS SNL — PART 1: INTRO**

**FADE IN:**

**INT. STUDIO 8H, MANHATTAN—NIGHT**

Painted saloon doors flank glitter curtains. Neon cactus hums. House band blends banjo twang, drum machine thump.

**ANNOUNCER (V.O.)**  
“Live from New York, it’s Saturday Night Live!”

Applause surges. Spotlight lands. **ARTHUR MORGAN** steps out—hat, worn coat, fresh mic pack, confused glare.

**ARTHUR**  
Evenin’. I was ridin’ west, then—bam—Manhattan. Y’all got streets packed tighter than Valentine on payday.

Crowd laughs. Arthur studies a cue card like it might bite.

**ARTHUR**  
Dutch said this gig meant “visibility.” Sounded like trouble. Turns out it’s jokes, cameras, strangers clappin’ on command. Kinda like a robbery, only nobody screams… much.

Beat. He tips hat.

**ARTHUR**  
I asked for a horse hitch. They offered “Uber.” I don’t know that fella, yet he took my money anyway.

Laughter. Band hits a jaunty sting.

Behind him, a giant screen shows cartoon “WANTED” posters: **DUTCH—CRIME: EXCESSIVE PLANNING**, **MICAH—CRIME: VIBES**, **UNCLE—CRIME: CHRONIC RESTING**.

**ARTHUR**  
We got sketches comin’. If anything goes wrong, blame time travel. If anything goes right, blame dumb luck.

He leans closer, stage-whisper.

**ARTHUR**  
Now… let’s do this civilized, before somebody suggests “one last plan.”

Arthur strides off. Applause rises again.

**CUT TO BLACK.**

prompt: Write about GoGoRiki  Rewrite your response. The last word of each sentence must become the first word of the next sentence.
response:
GoGoRiki is an animated series that began in Russia and spread worldwide.  
Worldwide audiences know it as Kikoriki or Smeshariki.  
Smeshariki features round characters who learn through funny adventures.  
Adventures mix humor with gentle lessons about friendship and problem-solving.  
Problem-solving often comes from the curious rabbit Krosh and his thoughtful friend Yozhik.  
Yozhik shares the village with Nyusha, Barash, Kopatych, Losyash, Pin, Sovunya, and Kar-Karych.  
Kar-Karych adds theatrical flair, while Losyash brings science and Pin brings inventive engineering.  
Engineering and creativity sit beside themes like empathy, responsibility, and respect for nature.  
Nature, community, and imagination have helped the franchise expand into films, games, and merchandise.  
Merchandise and translations carried the show far beyond its 2003 debut.  
Debut or not, GoGoRiki remains known for bright comedy that teaches without sounding preachy.

response:
- Weapon identity is strong: most classes are clearly anchored to a primary weapon type (axe/sword/spear/dagger/unarmed/spells/long range), and nearly every class has a “Mastery” skill that provides flat scaling bonuses (usually hit/crit/damage).

- Class stat packages generally match role: high STR/HP/VIG classes trend toward frontline damage (Berserker, Ansatsuken), high DEF/VIT classes trend toward tank/support (Shielder, Diamond Style), high AGI/DEX classes trend toward skirmish/ranged/assassination (Swordfighter, Archer, Assassin, Trickster).

- Many kits include a “proc passive” tied to two stats: Outrage (STR+VIG), Blade Dance (STR+DEX), Overwhelm (STR+LCK), Lethality (LCK+DEX), Wheel of Fate (INT+LCK), Aegis (VIT+DEF), Healing Aura (MAG+LCK). Pattern: a signature passive that reinforces the class’s growth priorities.

- Offense kits are more complete than utility kits: melee damage dealers have multiple ways to increase damage, hit multiple targets, or bypass defence/guard; several ranged and rogue-adjacent classes still have multiple “Unknown” placeholders, so utility/identity is uneven across the roster.

- Guard/defence interaction is a recurring system hook: Berserker ignores DEF, Ansatsuken punishes guard tiers, Shielder/Dimond Style build around guarding, Lancer disables guard, Swordfighter avoids counterattacks. This implies “guard play” is a core combat pillar worth supporting across more classes.

- AoE patterns repeat by archetype: axes and long range often get row/area attacks (Whirlwind, Arc Shot, Volley), while daggers tend to be single-target + debuff stacking, and unarmed tends to be multi-hit or positional (Raging Demon, Palm Burst).

- Resource identity is emerging but inconsistent: Berserker spends HP to spike damage, casters spend MP, many physical classes spend SP, but several skills list “Cost = XSP/XMP” which makes balancing and class feel hard to evaluate until costs are standardized.

- Counterplay hooks exist but are clustered: silence and debuff immunity appear (Throat Strike, Mana Circuit Disruption, Pure Field, Savage Fighter L3, Wary Fighter L3), but other common tactical counters (dispel enemy buffs, cleanse terrain effects, interrupt charging, anti-follow-up, anti-AoE) are sparse or absent.

- Gap: fewer defensive/mobility tools for fragile damage dealers compared to the amount of burst they can output; only some have safe reposition (Withdrawal) or “no counterattack” (Hastened Strike), while others (Sniper, Assassin) lack a clearly-defined escape/defense option in the listed skills.

- Gap: limited “team support” options outside Priest/Shielder/Diamond/Prophet; rogues and martial classes rarely provide buffs, formation tools, or ally-enabling effects (except Chain Attack / Pursuit style follow-ups).

- Suggested skills to fill gaps: Berserker “Blood Rush” (self-buff that grants +AGI or +movement for 1–2 turns but reduces DEF/RES, cost HP) to give controlled engage/disengage.

- Suggested skills to fill gaps: Swordfighter “Riposte Stance” (if attacked this turn, first counterattack gains +hit/+crit and ignores counter-counter mechanics) to deepen the duelist identity beyond pure offense.

- Suggested skills to fill gaps: Lancer “Pin Down” (on hit, applies a short-duration “cannot reposition/retreat” or reduces enemy movement/evasion) to give spears more control and frontliner utility.

- Suggested skills to fill gaps: Shielder “Shield Bash” (low damage + guaranteed Stun/Prone if target is guarding, or reduces guard tier) to let tanks actively disrupt instead of only absorbing.

- Suggested skills to fill gaps: Sniper “Camouflage” (enter a hidden/covered state: +evasion, cannot be targeted by long range beyond X tiles, broken when attacking) to define a survivability loop for a high-DEX class.

- Suggested skills to fill gaps: Sniper “Marked Target” (single-target debuff: marked enemy takes +hit against it from allies, or reveals its evasion/crit; synergizes with Steady Focus and Accurate Aim) to add party contribution.

- Suggested skills to fill gaps: Hunter “Skirmisher Swap” (after using a long range attack, can switch to axe stance granting +damage/guard break next turn; or vice versa) to lean into hybrid weapon identity.

- Suggested skills to fill gaps: Archer “Suppressing Fire” (row/area attack with lower damage but applies -hit or prevents counterattacks) to differentiate Archer from Hunter/Sniper as battlefield control ranged.

- Suggested skills to fill gaps: Gunner “Reload Discipline” (resource/tempo skill: spend a turn to gain +hit/+crit and reduce SP cost of the next 2 shot skills) to create a clear cadence for firearms.

- Suggested skills to fill gaps: Assassin “Smoke Bomb” (instant reposition + temporary evasion boost; breaks enemy lock/mark; optional blind in adjacent tiles) to prevent assassins from being one-and-done.

- Suggested skills to fill gaps: Thief “Steal” or “Mug” (chance to steal consumable/money; higher chance if target is debuffed/stunned) to reinforce the economic/utility fantasy beyond Profit.

- Suggested skills to fill gaps: Trickster “Bait and Switch” (swap positions with an ally in range; both gain evasion or the ally gains guard) to make Trickster a formation manipulator.

- Suggested skills to fill gaps: Ninja “Shuriken Fan” (small AoE ranged poke that applies minor bleed/poison or reduces hit) to give ninja a consistent ranged tool and status delivery.

- Suggested skills to fill gaps: Gentle Fist “Ki Guard” (convert MAG/RES into temporary damage reduction vs physical and magical for 1 turn) to offset low DEF growth and maintain the anti-mage brawler niche.

- Suggested skills to fill gaps: Ansatsuken “Focus Break” (on hit, interrupts charging/stance skills and drains SP) to create a distinct anti-technique martial identity.

- Suggested skills to fill gaps: Diamond Style “Bodyguard Anchor” (link to an ally: redirect a % of damage to self and grant ally debuff resistance; breaks if separated) to strengthen the protector archetype.

- Suggested skills to fill gaps: Priest “Dispel” (remove enemy buffs/stances/guards or reduce barrier values) to broaden support beyond healing/mitigation and give counterplay to defensive stacking.

- Suggested skills to fill gaps: Witch/Warlock “Hex Zone” (terrain/area curse: enemies entering or starting turn suffer -hit/-DEF/-RES) to add battlefield control rather than only single-target curses.

- Suggested skills to fill gaps: Prophet “Foretold Doom” (delayed effect mark: after 2 turns, target takes fixed damage or suffers a strong debuff; increases if the target misses/gets debuffed) to deepen the “future manipulation” theme.

- Suggested skills to fill gaps: Sage “Elemental Ward” (choose an element; allies in a row take reduced damage of that element and gain minor MP/SP recovery when hit by it) to make Sage feel like a hybrid sustain/element specialist rather than a duplicate statline.

- System-wide suggestion: add at least one “anti-follow-up / anti-proc” debuff somewhere (e.g., “Disrupted Rhythm: cannot trigger extra attacks/counters for 1 turn”) to balance proc-heavy kits like Swordfighter/Archer/Trickster.

- System-wide suggestion: standardize missing costs and scaling language (XSP/XMP, “same as normal attack” definitions, crit rules, and guard interaction) so class comparisons and skill-point valuation are consistent.

prompt: Write a descriptive, fictional, imaginative parody screenplay of Shinji Ikari hosting SNL. Part 1, introduction Rewrite your response. Use at least 2 different coordinating conjunctions in the response.
response:
Title: **Neon Genesis Evangelion: LIVE From Tokyo-3 (But Also New York)**  
**Part 1 — Introduction**

**INT. STUDIO 8H – SNL STAGE – NIGHT**

A familiar roar: the **SNL** audience, packed shoulder-to-shoulder, clapping like their rent depends on it. The band kicks up an upbeat, swingy parody of **“A Cruel Angel’s Thesis”**—all brass confidence and suspiciously dramatic percussion.

The camera glides past cue cards, stagehands, and a **giant foam prop** shaped like an Evangelion entry plug that absolutely should not fit through any door in this building.

**ANNOUNCER (V.O.)**  
Ladies and gentlemen… **Shinji Ikari!**

The curtain parts.

**SHINJI IKARI** steps out in a tailored suit that looks borrowed from someone who has never once been asked to “get in the robot.” He raises a hand in a tentative wave—like he’s trying to greet the crowd **and** apologize to it at the same time.

Polite applause surges into louder cheers, because audiences love a nervous host. Shinji blinks at the noise as if it’s a new kind of Angel.

**SHINJI**  
Uh—hi. Hello. I’m Shinji Ikari… and I’m hosting Saturday Night Live.

(beat; he tries to smile)  
That sentence feels… illegal.

Audience laughs.

**SHINJI (CONT’D)**  
So, um. I know what you’re thinking: “Wait, aren’t you the guy who pilots a biomechanical god-weapon?”  
And—yes. But tonight I’m doing something even more terrifying.

He gestures at the cameras.

**SHINJI (CONT’D)**  
Live comedy. No armor. No cockpit. Just… vibes and consequences.

A bigger laugh. Shinji nods, encouraged, then immediately looks worried about being encouraged.

**SHINJI (CONT’D)**  
Back home, if I mess up, my dad is disappointed. Here, if I mess up, **millions of people** are disappointed, **so** honestly it’s pretty similar.

More laughter. Shinji takes a cautious step forward, like he’s approaching a microphone that might bite.

Behind him, the set subtly reveals an **overly serious NERV-style control console**, except the monitors show **SNL graphics**, snack orders, and a blinking alert that reads: *LAUGH TRACK: OPTIONAL.*

**SHINJI (CONT’D)**  
They told me hosting SNL is like piloting an Eva. You need timing, you need rhythm, you need trust…

(he swallows)  
…**but** you also need to know where the bathroom is, because Studio 8H is huge and I’ve already gotten lost twice.

The audience cracks up. Shinji exhales, relieved, yet still visibly haunted by the concept of “hallways.”

**SHINJI (CONT’D)**  
Anyway, we have a great show tonight! Our musical guest is here—there are amazing sketches—there are… fewer traumatic flashbacks than usual.

(beat)  
No promises, **yet**.

He gives a small, earnest bow that’s half gratitude and half self-defense.

**SHINJI (CONT’D)**  
So stick around. I’m going to do my best. Please clap when appropriate. Please don’t deploy the spears.

He points awkwardly toward the camera with the energy of someone trying to be confident **and** politely asking the world not to collapse.

**SHINJI (CONT’D)**  
We’ll be right back!

**SMASH CUT TO BLACK.**  
The band hits a triumphant sting—big, brassy, absurdly heroic—like the show is about to save humanity from bad punchlines.

prompt: Acting as a liberated female writer create a short story told from the point of view of a girl who is going to present to her anatomy class about midwifery but is feeling embarrassed. Throughout the story she regrets dry cleaning her bodysuit uniform which grows tighter and tighter throughout the story and clings uncomfortably to her body. She is so stressed by this she mixes up the words for organs in the system associated with being a midwife so she makes up similar words. Differences before and during birth. The class goes along with it, accepting all of her nonsense words for body parts. While at first she did not like the bodysuit by the end she appreciates it as it allows her to nearly model the organs she is describing. At the end of the story however she is better able to model on herself with the suit off and gets an A+ from the teacher. Rewrite your response. Include exactly 3 numbers in the response.
response:
I regretted the dry cleaning the moment I zipped myself into the uniform.

The bodysuit had been fine yesterday—practical, official, the kind of garment meant to make us look like a team of future clinicians instead of a scatter of anxious students. But whatever heat, solvent, or spite lived inside that dry cleaner had changed it. The seams felt closer than they should. The fabric clung like it had learned my shape and decided to argue with it.

I stood outside the anatomy lab door and took 3 slow breaths, the kind we’re told to use in emergencies, as if embarrassment were a medical event. My presentation topic—midwifery—wasn’t embarrassing to me in private. In private I loved it: the steadiness of hands, the calm voice in a loud room, the way birth is both ordinary biology and a thunderstorm of meaning. What embarrassed me was saying it out loud to a room full of students trained to pounce on mistakes like they were extra credit.

Inside, the fluorescent lights made everything feel too visible. I could feel the bodysuit tightening as I walked, not because it was actually shrinking minute by minute, but because stress makes your own body swell against your clothes—lungs expanding, shoulders lifting, stomach holding its breath. I slid my note cards from my pocket and they stuck for a second, like even paper disapproved of my outfit.

“Ready when you are,” the teacher said.

I stepped to the front and faced my classmates. I could feel the suit pulling across my ribs when I raised my arms to point at the diagram on the screen. It gave me a posture I didn’t ask for—upright, displayed, pinned into place. My face went hot. Somewhere in my mind, the right vocabulary scattered like birds.

“Okay,” I began, trying for confident and getting something closer to polite panic. “Midwifery focuses on supporting the pregnant person before labor, during birth, and after delivery, with attention to—um—reproductive anatomy.”

So far, so good.

Then I saw the word on my slide: uterus.

My mouth, betrayed by pressure and polyester, said, “The… use-terror.”

Silence.

I expected laughter. I expected correction. I expected my teacher to stop me the way you stop someone walking confidently toward the wrong train.

Instead, someone in the second row nodded, taking notes like I had just revealed a sacred term.

“Yes,” I continued, startled into momentum. “The use-terror is the muscular organ that… holds the pregnancy and contracts in labor.” I pointed to my lower abdomen with a hand that felt too visible because the bodysuit made every gesture look deliberate. “Before birth, it’s mostly expanding and accommodating. During birth, it’s doing coordinated contractions to move the baby downward.”

I glanced at my next label: cervix.

My tongue went soft again. “The service,” I said. “The service is the lower part that stays closed and firm during pregnancy, then softens and opens during labor.”

More nodding. Pens kept moving. No one blinked. It was like the whole room had quietly agreed that my nonsense words were the official language of women’s bodies, and honestly—wasn’t that a little bit true? How many times had perfectly real anatomy been renamed, blurred, euphemized, made strange to keep it from sounding powerful?

The bodysuit tightened again when I inhaled, and I hated it for a fresh second. It felt like being wrapped in someone else’s expectations: neat, contained, unwrinkled. I had wanted to talk about midwifery like it was normal—like it belonged in a lab and in a conversation, not hidden behind jokes or whispers. And here I was, tripping over terms like my own mouth had been dry cleaned too.

I clicked to the next slide and saw placenta.

“Here,” I said, “is the pleasant-a.”

A little ripple of appreciation went through the class, as if I’d made a clever pun on purpose.

“The pleasant-a is the temporary organ that exchanges oxygen and nutrients,” I went on, grateful that I still remembered the function even if the name had skidded sideways. “Before birth, it’s the connection. During birth, after the baby is out, the pleasant-a is delivered too, and we monitor bleeding and uterine tone to prevent hemorrhage.”

I kept going. Amniotic sac became the “arm-knee-otic wrap.” Perineum turned into the “peri-neighborhood.” I talked about how care differs before and during birth: how prenatal visits focus on screening, education, nutrition, mental health, and building trust; how intrapartum care shifts to monitoring vital signs, contraction patterns, fetal well-being, pain management options, and the emotional temperature of the room.

And the whole time, the bodysuit kept insisting on itself—pressing at my thighs when I shifted my weight, pulling at my shoulders when I gestured, hugging my waist like it wanted to win an argument with my lungs. I kept thinking, Why did I do that? Why did I dry clean it? I could have hand-washed it like a normal person. I could have worn literally anything else.

But something odd happened as I talked.

Because the fabric was so unforgiving, it made me aware of my own physical map. When I described the “use-terror,” my hand naturally settled low and central. When I mentioned where the “service” sits, my fingers indicated the change in angle of my pelvis. When I spoke about how midwives watch for signs of progress—how the body opens and shifts and makes room—my movements became clearer, more anatomical, less like flailing and more like demonstration.

I didn’t like the bodysuit, but I couldn’t deny it: it turned my torso into a kind of simplified model, a smooth surface for showing where things were without getting lost in loose fabric. It made my gestures readable.

I clicked forward and saw a slide about stages of labor. I had rehearsed this part. I could do this part.

Then I felt the bodysuit pinch at my ribs, sharply, like it was reminding me who was in charge.

My brain blanked.

I stared at my note card and, for no reason I could explain, I began talking about the “dilation situation” and the “descension dimension,” as if rhyming would keep my confidence from falling apart. A boy in the back wrote it down with complete seriousness. My teacher watched me with an expression that wasn’t mocking; it was interested, the way clinicians look when they’re deciding whether a weird presentation is actually a useful variation.

Halfway through, I realized I was spending so much energy fighting the suit that I was losing the point: my voice. My knowledge. My right to stand here and speak plainly about bodies that create life.

I stopped. The clicker in my hand felt slick.

“I need a second,” I said, and then, because my body was screaming for mercy, I added, “This uniform shrank. I can’t breathe in it.”

No laughter. Just a collective, human understanding—because everyone has had clothes betray them at the worst time.

Behind the side cabinet where the lab coats hung, I unzipped and stepped out of the bodysuit. Underneath, I had a simple tank top and leggings—still classroom-appropriate, still me, only now I could expand when I inhaled. I walked back out holding the bodysuit folded over my arm like a shed skin.

I felt taller without it.

I returned to the front, exhaled, and looked at my classmates again. My hands were steadier now, and when I demonstrated anatomy, I didn’t need the suit’s tight lines to make my gestures clear. I used my own landmarks—ribs, hips, the curve of my abdomen—and I spoke like I actually belonged in the room.

“To be precise,” I said, glancing at the slide and then back at them, “it’s the uterus, the cervix, the placenta, the amniotic sac. Before birth, the goal is health and preparation. During birth, the goal is safety and support, moment to moment—while respecting the laboring person’s choices, pain, dignity, and autonomy.”

I flipped to slide 2 and finished the last section without inventing any new vocabulary at all.

At the end, my teacher didn’t comment on the earlier word chaos. She just held my gaze the way she did when someone finally landed the idea.

“A+,” she said. “And thank you for modeling consent and self-advocacy in real time.”

As I sat down, the bodysuit folded on my lap, I thought about how it had tried to contain me—how I’d tried to contain myself. I had walked in wishing I could disappear, and I walked out knowing something quieter and stronger: I didn’t need a uniform to be credible. I needed breath, knowledge, and the nerve to take up space.

And if I had to count it, I’d say the turning point was 1 choice: stepping out of the thing that was squeezing my voice, and speaking anyway.

prompt: Write a story where a rabbit sees legs sticking out of a pool of grey, thick, gooey, bubbling mud, completely covered in the thick substance  Rewrite your response. Ensure that stop words constitute no more than 29% of the total words in your response.
response:
Morning fog drifts across Whispering Woods. Rabbit Toby scouts marsh fringe, nose twitching, paws silent. Air tastes metallic, sour, wet.

Ahead, willow shadows frame trouble: legs sticking out of a pool of grey, thick, gooey, bubbling mud, completely covered in the thick substance. No fur visible. No feathers visible. Just two slick columns, mud-sheathed, trembling, then still.

Mud surface heaves. Bubbles rise, burst, spit grey blisters. Each pop sounds like a swallowed gulp. Toby freezes, heart drumbeat, ears angled forward. No shout. No pleading. Only gurgle, suck, sigh.

Toby backs away, scans ground, finds alder branch, thick, forked. He creeps near pool edge, tests soil, avoids soft spots. Branch tip pokes one muddy shin. Nothing. Second poke, harder.

Legs jerk. Mud tightens, hungry, dragging downward. Toby drops branch, grabs long vine, twists loop, flings loop around one ankle, then second ankle, cinches knot with teeth. He braces hind paws against root, pulls, claws digging grooves.

Suction fights back. Mud stretches, strings, snaps. Another pull—harder—until one violent squelch releases trapped body. Grey mass slumps onto grass.

Mud slides off face, revealing young heron, blinking, coughing, chest heaving. Heron croaks thanks, voice thin, shaken. Toby nudges heron toward creek, steady, watchful. Cold water peels mud away, bubble by bubble.

Later, Toby hops home, mind replaying image: grey bubbling trap; two mud-coated legs; silent danger; small rabbit strength, stubborn rescue.

- **Headline:** Andrew Marr shocks viewers with unusually loud, assertive interview style on live broadcast

- **Lead:** A live political discussion featuring veteran broadcaster Andrew Marr took an unexpected turn this week when he departed from his typically measured tone, repeatedly raising his voice and forcefully pressing guests for direct answers—moments that quickly spread across social media and reignited debate about how aggressively journalists should challenge public figures.

- **What happened on air:** Viewers watching the episode described an uncharacteristically confrontational Marr, who interrupted more often than usual, rejected vague responses, and insisted guests address contradictions and specifics rather than pivoting to talking points.

- **Key exchange that went viral:** One segment drawing particular attention involved Marr challenging a politician over inconsistencies in public statements on environmental policy. According to clips circulating online, Marr demanded a clear explanation and refused to move on until the guest addressed the discrepancy, leaving the interviewee visibly rattled.

- **Studio atmosphere:** Audience members and commentators noted a tense dynamic as other guests appeared more cautious, pausing before answering and attempting to steer the conversation back toward broader themes—efforts Marr repeatedly cut through by returning to his original questions.

- **Public reaction:** Responses split sharply. Supporters applauded the tougher approach, arguing that evasive answers have become too common and that sharper interviewing is necessary for accountability. Critics said the raised volume and rapid interruptions undermined constructive debate and crossed into unnecessary hostility.

- **Commentary from media analysts:** Several broadcast observers framed the moment as part of a wider shift in political interviewing, where presenters face pressure to be more combative in order to cut through rehearsed messaging—while also risking accusations of bias or performative confrontation.

- **Marr’s response:** In remarks posted after the episode, Marr defended the need for clarity and accountability in interviews, saying that pressing for straightforward answers is essential—while maintaining that respect for guests and viewers should remain central to the format.

- **What it means next:** Whether the episode marks a one-off flashpoint or a deliberate change in tone remains unclear, but the broadcast has already prompted renewed discussion about the balance between civility and scrutiny in modern political journalism.

prompt: Write about Operation Rwanda  Rewrite your response. The response must start with a verb.
response:
Explain Operation Rwanda—more commonly known as **France’s Operation Turquoise**—as a UN-authorized military intervention launched in **June 1994** during the **Rwandan genocide**, and note that it remains highly controversial because its humanitarian claims and political effects are still debated.

### Context
Situate the operation within the genocide that unfolded after the **6 April 1994** plane crash that killed President **Juvénal Habyarimana**, which was followed by mass killings led by extremist elements of the Rwandan government and militias, targeting mainly **Tutsi** and also **moderate Hutu**. Roughly **hundreds of thousands** of people were murdered over about **100 days**.

### UN authorization and stated aims
Describe how the **UN Security Council (Resolution 929, June 1994)** authorized a French-led force to conduct a temporary intervention with a stated goal of **protecting civilians**, facilitating **humanitarian relief**, and helping stabilize areas affected by violence.

### Deployment and “safe zone”
Report that France deployed about **2,500 troops** (with limited multinational participation) primarily in **southwestern Rwanda**, establishing a protected area often called the **“Zone Turquoise.”** Many civilians sought refuge there, and the operation is credited by supporters with saving lives in areas it controlled.

### Major controversies
Outline why the operation is disputed:
- **Late timing:** it began after much of the killing had already occurred, limiting its ability to stop the genocide overall.
- **Perceived partiality:** critics cite France’s prior political and military ties with Rwanda’s former government and argue the operation was not fully neutral.
- **Escape routes for perpetrators:** allegations persist that the operation, intentionally or not, enabled some genocide perpetrators to **flee into what was then Zaire (now the DRC)**, complicating later efforts at accountability and contributing to regional instability.

### Legacy
Conclude that Operation Turquoise is remembered both as a **humanitarian intervention that protected some civilians** and as a **politically fraught mission** whose broader impact—especially regarding neutrality and post-genocide consequences—continues to be debated by historians, governments, and survivors.

It proposes relocating some people who arrive in the UK through irregular routes to Rwanda for their asylum claims to be processed. Supporters argue it will deter dangerous Channel crossings and weaken smuggling networks, but does deterrence justify transferring asylum seekers to a third country? Under the plan, Rwanda would assess protection claims under its domestic procedures and stated international commitments. People granted refugee status would be supported to settle in Rwanda rather than in the UK. How robust are the practical safeguards in Rwanda around legal advice, fair hearings, and long-term integration? The UK also committed significant funding to Rwanda linked to implementing the partnership and building capacity. Human rights organisations and refugee advocates say the scheme risks unfair outcomes and potential onward removal, and they question Rwanda’s human-rights protections. Can the policy be made compatible with the Refugee Convention, the European Convention on Human Rights, and UK public-law requirements? UK litigation, including a Supreme Court ruling, found serious concerns about safety and the risk of wrongful removal, which stalled flights. The UK government then pursued a new treaty and domestic legislation intended to designate Rwanda as a safe country for removals. prompt: how can a climaxfinale/ending to a story in a game, truly feel like one? Rewrite your response. Your answer must contain at least two sentences ending in a period followed by at least two bullet points denoted by *.
response:
A game finale truly feels like a climax when it’s the earned peak of everything the player has learned, feared, wanted, and fought for. It should deliver a moment of maximum tension and meaning, then allow enough aftermath to make the victory, loss, or choice land.

* Build escalating stakes and clear payoff: foreshadow key elements, tighten the conflict, and make the ending resolve the most important promises the story made.  
* Close character arcs in a satisfying way: show how the protagonist (and major allies/rivals) changed, and let their choices matter in the final outcome.  
* Make the final gameplay test feel “ultimate”: remix core mechanics into a harder, more dramatic challenge (boss/puzzle/decision gauntlet) that proves mastery rather than introducing random new rules.  
* Merge story and player agency: ensure the player’s actions, builds, relationships, and earlier decisions visibly shape the climax and its consequences.  
* Use presentation to elevate emotion: music, pacing, camera/visual framing, and environmental changes should all signal “this is the moment” without relying only on cutscenes.  
* Provide resolution plus breathing room: answer key questions, show consequences, and give a short epilogue or reflective scene so the ending feels complete rather than abrupt.

### Top 4 Football Skill Moves for a Defender (With Tutorials)

#### 1) Jockeying (Contain & Control)
**Why it’s great:** It helps you delay the attacker **and** keep them away from dangerous areas.

**Tutorial:**
1. Get into a low, balanced stance (knees bent, chest slightly forward).
2. Stay side-on so you can move backward or sideways quickly.
3. Take small, quick steps to match the attacker’s speed.
4. Keep your body between the attacker and the goal, **but** don’t stab at the ball too early.
5. When the attacker takes a heavier touch, step in to challenge.

---

#### 2) Standing Tackle (Poke/Block Tackle)
**Why it’s great:** It wins the ball cleanly **or** forces a mistake without over-committing.

**Tutorial:**
1. Close down under control—don’t sprint straight in.
2. Time it for when the ball is slightly away from the attacker’s foot.
3. Use your front foot to poke the ball away, then immediately recover your balance.
4. If you can’t poke it, use your body to block the path and force the attacker to stop.
5. After winning it, take your first touch away from pressure **so** you can pass safely.

---

#### 3) Body Feint / Shoulder Drop (Escape Pressure)
**Why it’s great:** It creates space to dribble out **yet** keeps the move simple and safe.

**Tutorial:**
1. Dribble slowly as the attacker approaches to invite pressure.
2. Drop one shoulder and shift your weight like you’re going that way.
3. Plant your outside foot, then push the ball the opposite way with your other foot.
4. Accelerate for 2–3 steps to make the feint “stick.”
5. Lift your head and play the safe pass or carry into space.

---

#### 4) Cruyff Turn (Turn Out of Trouble)
**Why it’s great:** It helps you turn away from pressure **and** keep the ball protected.

**Tutorial:**
1. Approach the ball as if you’re going to pass or cross with your inside foot.
2. Swing your leg like you’re striking the ball, **but** instead drag the ball behind your standing leg with the inside of that foot.
3. Rotate your hips and shoulders as you pull the ball back.
4. Take your next touch into the space behind you (away from the defender).
5. Burst away and make the next pass quickly.

---

If you tell me your position (CB, RB/LB, or CDM) and whether you’re right- or left-footed, I can tailor which side to execute each move on and when to use it in a match.

prompt: help me make a challenge in scrap mechinc. i want it to be about a car parking in different spaces Rewrite your response. Use at least 173 unique words in the response.
response:
Build a Scrap Mechanic “precision driver” challenge where the goal is to place a car neatly into multiple marked bays, each with a different twist. Start by deciding a theme (training yard, rooftop garage, shipping dock) and sketch a route that flows from one slot to the next without long dead time.

**1) Course layout**
- Make 6–10 stations: wide beginner stalls, angled bays, parallel curb spots, narrow alley pull-ins, a U-turn box, and a final “one-try” garage door entry.  
- Vary surfaces: concrete for grip, dirt for wobble, wedges for camber, a short ramp for uphill starts, and a slick segment using low-friction blocks if you like.

**2) Clear rules**
- The car must stop fully inside painted lines; wheels cannot touch boundary blocks.  
- Add penalties for cone hits, wall taps, or reversing more than a set number of times.  
- Optional time limit per station to create tension.

**3) Vehicle constraints**
- Set maximum width/length, plus a minimum turning requirement.  
- Ban thrusters for a realistic feel, or require suspension and functioning brake lights for style points.  
- Allow adjustable steering using bearings and controllers.

**4) Scoring and feedback**
- Use logic gates, timers, and sensors (seat sensor + contact sensor plates) to detect “car present” and “fully stopped.”  
- A scoreboard can be simple: lights showing bronze/silver/gold, or a counter displaying attempts.

**5) Difficulty modifiers**
- Moving barriers driven by pistons, rotating arms, a narrowing gate, or a brief blackout section with lamps toggled by switches.  
- Add a “precision stop” zone: front bumper must align with a marker.

**6) Test and iterate**
Drive every bay with a basic build, then with a longer vehicle. Adjust line width, obstacle spacing, and camera visibility until it feels challenging but fair.

My Answer: To net $100k/month from producing fully finished, professional songs, you’ll need (1) high-ticket offers, (2) scalable products/licensing, and (3) consistent lead generation. A workable approach is to build 3–5 revenue streams and design them to hit the target with realistic math:

1) Productize a high-ticket “done-for-you song” offer (fastest path)  
- Offer: “Radio-ready song package” (writing + production + mix + master + optional vocal sourcing) with clear deliverables, turnaround time, revisions, and usage rights.  
- Pricing examples: $7,500–$20,000 per song depending on scope (exclusive rights cost more).  
- Goal math: 10 clients/month at $10k = $100k gross (you’ll need margin control via templates, assistants, and tight revision policies).  
- Key: specialize in outcomes (e.g., “TikTok-optimized pop hooks,” “label-ready EDM,” “brand anthem for companies”) and show a portfolio that proves it.

2) Scale with sync licensing (high upside, slower ramp)  
- Build a sync catalog: 100–300 tracks across ad-friendly genres (uplifting pop, tension beds, corporate, trap, etc.).  
- Pitch to: music libraries, supervisors, and agencies; or use a sync agent.  
- Structure: keep clean metadata, stems, alt mixes, and clear split sheets.  
- Revenue: a few strong placements can be $5k–$50k+ each; recurring backend royalties can compound.

3) Sell “semi-custom” songs and production packs (mid-ticket scalable)  
- Offer: pre-built “song shells” or “customizable topline-ready tracks.”  
- Pricing: $500–$3,000 each depending on exclusivity and included stems.  
- Goal math: 50 sales/month at $1,000 = $50k gross (paired with your high-ticket work).

4) Monthly retainers for creators/brands (stability)  
- Offer: 4–8 tracks/month for a creator network, YouTube channels, podcasts, or small agencies.  
- Pricing: $3k–$15k/month per client depending on volume and exclusivity.  
- Goal math: 8 retainers at $12.5k = $100k gross, or 5 retainers at $10k = $50k plus other streams.

5) Direct-response marketing + outbound (the engine)

  - Alyx (hallucination): “That’s not strategy anymore. That’s punishment.”

- **Collaborations:** Collaborating With Other Artists Or Influencers Can Expose Your Services To A Broader Audience.

- **Understand Client Needs:** Communication Is Key. Ensure You Fully Understand What Your Client Wants And Deliver Accordingly. This Might Involve Revisions And Feedback Loops.

- **Build A Brand:** As Demand Grows, Consider Building A Brand Around Your Service. This Could Eventually Lead To Passive Income Streams Through Digital Products Like Sample Packs Or Instructional Content.  

Creating And Selling Custom Songs Requires Not Only Musical Talent And Production Skills But Also A Knack For Marketing And Customer Service. With Dedication And Hard Work, It’s Entirely Possible To Build A Lucrative Business In This Creative Field.

prompt: Why would i be seen as a idiot if i made a INSANELY well made live event just for the game to delete itsself after the lvie event ends. Rewrite your response. The response must start with a verb.
response:
Recognize that making an insanely well-made live event isn’t the “idiot” part—the part that can make you *look* foolish is the *decision and messaging* around the game deleting itself afterward.

- **Waste perceived value**: People will see it as throwing away something you proved you could build, especially if it took major time, money, or talent to make.
- **Frustrate your players**: If players got attached, spent money, or invested hours, deleting the game can feel like betrayal or a scam unless it was clearly promised from the start.
- **Kill momentum**: A great live event usually boosts interest, retention, and word-of-mouth. Deleting the game immediately can look like you didn’t understand (or didn’t care about) what makes live events worthwhile.
- **Trigger backlash and ridicule**: Streamers, friends, and social media tend to dunk on choices that seem self-sabotaging or “for shock value,” even if the event itself was top-tier.
- **Signal unreliability**: Future players may assume your next project could vanish too, which makes them less likely to download, pay, or commit.

If you *want* the “one-night-only” vibe, the key is to **communicate it upfront**, give players a way to **preserve memories** (recordings, replays, rewards that carry over), and make the deletion feel like an **intentional artistic statement** rather than a surprise punishment.

prompt: Write a story where a man is arrested and told "You're gonna be late for prison if you don't move" Rewrite your response. Write the entire response in title case (capitalize the first letter of every major word).
response:
Daniel Wright Hated Mornings That Started Quietly.

Quiet Meant Time To Think, And Thinking Meant Counting. Mortgage. Car Payment. The New Dent In The Fridge Door From When He’d Tried To Carry Too Much In One Trip. He Preferred Noise—A Podcast, The Kettle Screaming, Anything That Kept His Mind From Wandering Into The Dark Little Corners.

That Tuesday, The World Held Its Breath.

He Stood In His Kitchen In A Wrinkled Dress Shirt, One Cuff Unbuttoned, Coffee Cooling In A Mug That Read BEST DAD, A Joke Gift From A Coworker Who Didn’t Know Daniel Didn’t Have Kids. Outside, The Streetlights Still Glowed, And A Thin Mist Slept On The Lawns Like It Had No Intention Of Leaving.

Then Came The Knock.

Not The Polite Tap Of A Neighbor. Not The Hesitant Rap Of A Delivery Driver. This Was Confident. Official. Three Blunt Strikes That Said Whoever Stood On The Other Side Already Knew How This Would Go.

Daniel Froze Long Enough To Hear A Second Knock, Then A Voice, Calm And Flat.

“Police. Open Up.”

He Set The Mug Down Too Carefully, As If Sudden Motion Might Break Something More Than Ceramic. He Crossed The Living Room, Past The Unread Mail, Past The Shoe He’d Kicked Off Last Night, And Opened The Door.

Two Officers Filled The Frame. One Was Tall And Square, With A Buzz Cut And A Face That Didn’t Invite Negotiation. The Other Looked Younger, His Eyes Moving Over The Doorway Like He Was Memorizing It.

“Daniel Wright?” The Tall One Asked.

“Yes,” Daniel Said. “What’s This About?”

The Tall Officer Didn’t Answer. He Reached Into His Jacket And Produced A Folder. Paper Edges, A Glimpse Of A Photo, The Sharp Flash Of A Badge Clip.

“Daniel Wright,” He Said Again, Like Repetition Made It Official, “You’re Under Arrest.”

Daniel Laughed Once, A Short, Wrong Sound. “That’s Not Funny. I Have Work In—”

“Turn Around,” The Younger Officer Said, Softer Than The Words Deserved.

“For What?” Daniel’s Voice Rose, Cracking Into Something He Didn’t Recognize. “Tell Me What I Did.”

The Tall Officer Stepped Forward. His Hand Found Daniel’s Wrist With The Casual Certainty Of A Man Who Had Done This A Thousand Times. Metal Clicked, Cold And Final.

“We Can Explain It At The Station,” The Tall Officer Said. Then, As If They Were Running Late For A Dentist Appointment Instead Of A Disaster, He Added, “You’re gonna be late for prison if you don’t move.”

The Sentence Landed Like A Brick Dropped Into Still Water. Prison. Not Jail. Not Questioning. Prison, As If The Verdict Had Already Happened Somewhere Daniel Wasn’t Allowed To Be.

Daniel Tried To Pull Back On Reflex. The Grip Tightened. The Younger Officer Looked Away, Like He’d Seen That Reflex Before And Didn’t Want To Watch It Die.

Daniel Was Guided Down His Front Steps. The Air Outside Felt Sharper Than It Had A Minute Ago, Like The World Had Tilted And All The Edges Had Become Blades. A Patrol Car Waited At The Curb, Engine Idling, Back Door Open As If It Had Been Hungry.

Neighbors’ Curtains Twitched. Someone’s Porch Light Flicked On. Daniel Thought Of Saying Something—Anything That Would Explain This, Anything That Would Make Him Look Less Like The Thing People Whispered About Later. But His Mouth Couldn’t Find The Right Shape.

They Put Him In The Back Seat.

The Door Closed With A Sound That Wasn’t Just A Door. It Was A Period. It Was A Lock Turning In A Place Inside His Chest.

As The Car Pulled Away, Daniel Leaned Forward Until The Seatbelt Cut Into His Shoulder. “This Is A Mistake,” He Said. “You Have The Wrong Guy. I’ve Never—”

The Tall Officer Drove Without Looking Back. “Save It For Intake.”

“Intake?” Daniel Repeated.

The Younger Officer Finally Met His Eyes In The Rearview Mirror. For A Second, There Was Something Human There—A Flicker Of Doubt, Or Pity, Or Exhaustion. Then His Face Smoothed Over Again. Professional.

At The Station, Everything Moved Too Fast And Too Slow At The Same Time. Daniel Was Led Through Doors That Buzzed Open Like Mechanical Sighs. He Was Asked Questions By People Who Didn’t Wait For Answers. His Belt Was Taken. His Shoelaces. His Wallet. His Watch—A Gift From His Father, Heavy And Reliable.

He Watched It Slide Into A Plastic Bin Like It Belonged To Someone Else.

A Fingerprint Scanner Lit His Hands An Unforgiving Green. A Camera Captured His Face Under Fluorescent Lights That Made Everyone Look Guilty. Daniel Tried To Stand Straight, Tried To Look Like A Man Who Would Be Cleared Any Second Now.

No One Looked At Him Like That Was Possible.

In A Small Interview Room, A Detective With A Coffee-Stained Tie Sat Across From Him And Opened The Same Folder The Tall Officer Had Held.

“You Know Why You’re Here?” The Detective Asked.

“No,” Daniel Said, Voice Hoarse. “And I Want A Lawyer.”

The Detective Nodded As If That Was Fine, As If This Was A Normal Conversation Between Reasonable People. Then He Turned The Folder Around.

A Photo Of A Man On A Security Camera. Grainy. Hood Up. Eyes Shadowed. The Man Held Something Long And Dark In His Hands. A Bar. A Pipe. A Gun, Maybe. The Background Looked Like The Back Of A Pharmacy.

Under The Photo Was A Name: Daniel Wright. Under That, A Date Of Birth. Under That, An Address.

His Address.

“That’s Not Me,” Daniel Said Immediately. “That’s Not Me. I Was Home That Night. I Was—”

“You Have Anyone Who Can Confirm That?” The Detective Asked.

Daniel Opened His Mouth And Realized The Answer Was No.

He Lived Alone. He Went To Work, He Went To The Store, He Paid His Bills. He Was The Kind Of Person Who Could Disappear Into Routine So Completely That No One Would Notice Until The Mail Piled Up.

The Detective Watched Him Understand That.

“Here’s The Thing,” The Detective Said, Leaning Back. “We’ve Got A String Of Robberies. Same Method. Same Build. And Your Prints Came Back On A Register Drawer.”

Daniel Felt The Room Tilt. “That’s Impossible.”

“It’s Not Impossible,” The Detective Said. “It’s Paperwork.”

Daniel Blinked. “What Does That Mean?”

“It Means Your Name Is In A System That Doesn’t Like Mistakes,” The Detective Said. “It Means Once The Machine Starts Moving, It Doesn’t Stop Because One Gear Thinks It Should.”

A Public Defender Met Him For Eight Minutes In A Hallway. Eight Minutes To Learn Daniel’s Entire Life And Translate It Into Legal Language. Eight Minutes To Say Words Like BAIL HEARING And PLEA and EVIDENCE CHAIN.

Eight Minutes To Look Tired Before The Fight Even Started.

By That Evening, Daniel Was In A Holding Cell With A Bench That Smelled Like Bleach And Despair. By The Next Morning, He Was In A Bus With Blacked-Out Windows, Hands Cuffed To A Chain That Linked Him To Men Who Didn’t Ask Questions Because Questions Were A Luxury.

He Tried To Think Of A Way Out. He Tried To Think Of Who Could Help. He Tried To Think Of How To Prove A Negative, How To Prove That In A World Full Of Cameras And Databases, Sometimes A Name Was Just A Name And A Fingerprint Was Just A Smudge On Someone Else’s Story.

When The Bus Stopped, A Guard Yelled Numbers Like He Was Calling Inventory.

Daniel Stepped Down Into A Yard Of Concrete And Razor Wire. The Sky Above Was Bright And Indifferent. The Air Carried The Faint Metallic Taste Of Something Permanent.

A Man In A Gray Uniform Ahead Of Him Looked Back And Smirked. “First Time?”

Daniel Didn’t Answer. He Could Still Hear The Tall Officer’s Voice, Casual And Certain, As If The Future Had Already Been Scheduled.

You’re gonna be late for prison if you don’t move.

Daniel Moved.

Not Because He Believed Them. Not Because He Understood. But Because The Machine Was Moving, And Every Door Behind Him Had Already Clicked Shut.

**(Fictional) Nintendo’s “Switch Transition” Sparks Outrage After Legacy Consoles Display Unskippable Farewell Message**

**KYOTO, Japan —** What began as a routine Tuesday firmware notification has, within forty‑eight hours, turned into the most bewildering consumer-tech controversy the games industry has seen in years. Across multiple regions, owners of the Wii, Wii U, and Nintendo 3DS report their systems abruptly booting into a stark, white screen featuring a single line of text: **“It’s time to move on to Nintendo Switch.”** No menu. No settings. No health-and-safety splash. Just the message, centered like an ultimatum.

Players describe the moment as “surreal,” “melancholy,” and “a hard reset of childhood.” In Minneapolis, teacher and longtime fan **Rita Alvarez** said her Wii U “worked fine Sunday night,” but Monday morning it would only show the sentence, refusing disc reads and ignoring controller inputs. “It felt like my console had been repossessed by a slogan,” she said.

Online, the phenomenon is being called **“The Curtain Call Update.”** Conspiracy threads, teardown videos, and packet captures have proliferated, with amateur investigators claiming the lockout resembles a remotely triggered “final state” rather than a random malfunction. A handful of modders allege the trigger is tied to a recently reactivated telemetry endpoint, though none of the claims have been independently verified.

Then came the second act.

Multiple households in the United States, Canada, and parts of Western Europe report unexpected doorstep visits from a representative carrying a slim clipboard and a hard plastic crate lined with foam. The visitor—typically dressed in a neat jacket with a minimal **red “S” pin**—allegedly introduces himself as a **“Nintendo Transition Courier.”** Several residents say he politely but firmly requests the old hardware, offering a printed receipt and a brochure detailing a “streamlined pathway” to the Switch ecosystem.

One Denver resident, **Mark Delling**, said the man knew the serial number of his Wii. “He didn’t threaten me,” Delling explained, “but he stood there like a cable technician who already has the work order closed. He told me, ‘We can do this the easy way: we take the system, and you start fresh.’”

Adding fuel to the uproar, a glossy new advertising campaign is appearing on bus shelters, pre-roll video, and billboard placements near shopping centers. The headline, set over a montage of starry skies dissolving into bright cityscapes, reads: **“Goodbye Galaxy, Hello Odyssey.”** The spot lingers on iconic imagery—spinning stars, familiar menu music—before cutting sharply to Switch footage and a tagline urging players to “leave the past playable, not primary.”

Marketing analysts note the phrase is an obvious wink at Nintendo’s own history, but critics argue the messaging lands as a taunt when paired with reports of forced lockouts. “It’s nostalgia weaponized,” said **Dr. Helen Mosier**, a media studies lecturer who researches fan communities. “You don’t get to sell memory as a product while simultaneously confiscating the objects that hold it.”

Nintendo’s official statement, released through a short press bulletin, does not directly confirm remote access or collection visits, but it does acknowledge what it calls a **“Legacy Platform Transition Initiative.”** The company writes: “As we evolve our services and focus on the best experiences for players, we are encouraging users to explore Nintendo Switch. We understand the affection people have for prior platforms and are committed to making the transition as smooth as possible.”

That phrasing has done little to calm anger. Consumer rights advocates are now questioning whether any forced disabling—if true—could violate regional regulations concerning digital ownership, device functionality, and post-sale support. **Amira Kwan**, an attorney specializing in technology policy, said the scenario would be “legally explosive” if a manufacturer intentionally rendered purchased hardware unusable outside narrow safety grounds. “A company can sunset online services,” Kwan noted. “Bricking a device to display a marketing message is another category entirely.”

Retailers are already feeling the aftershocks. Several shops report a sudden spike in Switch demand, plus an odd secondary trend: shoppers asking for “proof” that a Switch will not someday receive the same treatment. Meanwhile, collectors are scrambling to isolate older consoles from networks, swapping tips about unplugging Wi‑Fi modules, storing systems in Faraday bags, or running them permanently offline.

On gaming forums, reactions range from grim jokes to genuine heartbreak. One post, widely shared, reads: “I paid for a library, not a countdown.” Others accuse Nintendo of trying to rewrite its own back catalog by force, compressing decades of eclectic experimentation into a single modern storefront.

As of press time, reports continue to arrive from additional cities, and the identity of the so-called courier remains unclear—employee, contractor, or prankster. What is certain is that the phrase **“It’s time to move on to Nintendo Switch”** has become less of a suggestion and more of a flashpoint.

Whether this episode becomes a cautionary tale about corporate control, a misunderstood rollout gone wrong, or the most audacious platform migration in entertainment history, one thing is undeniable: in living rooms around the world, the past has begun to blink out—replaced by a sentence that refuses to be ignored.

prompt: Imagine yourself a YouTuber and tell me The importance of reading to change bad habits Rewrite your response. Ensure that stop words constitute no more than 52% of the total words in your response.
response:
[Camera on, quick hook]

Bad habits survive on autopilot. Reading breaks autopilot.

Here’s why reading matters when you want real habit change—and how to use it like a tool, not “motivation.”

## 1) Reading creates awareness
Bad habit = cue → craving → response → reward.  
Books give language for patterns: triggers, routines, payoffs. Once pattern becomes visible, change becomes possible.

## 2) Reading upgrades identity
Habit change sticks when identity shifts: “I’m a runner,” “I’m a non‑smoker,” “I’m a focused creator.”  
Stories, memoirs, psychology books: repeated exposure to growth identities, stronger self-image, better choices.

## 3) Reading supplies replacement behaviors
Quitting “cold turkey” fails because brain wants reward.  
Reading offers replacement actions: journaling, breathwork, walking, time-blocking, phone-free routines. Bad habit loses slot; good habit fills slot.

## 4) Reading strengthens attention (anti-impulse training)
Scrolling trains distraction. Reading trains focus.  
More focus = more pause before impulse = more control during craving peaks.

## 5) Reading lowers shame, raises agency
Learning: relapse cycles, stress responses, dopamine loops.  
Understanding reduces self-attack. Agency increases: “Problem = system,” not “Problem = me.”

## 6) Reading gives practical systems
Great books deliver frameworks: implementation intentions, habit stacking, environment design, friction, rewards, tracking. Systems beat willpower.

---

# 10-minute “reading for habit change” routine
1. Pick one target habit: smoking, junk food, doomscrolling.  
2. Read 5–10 pages daily.  
3. Highlight one tactic.  
4. Write one sentence plan: “If cue happens, I will do replacement.”  
5. Run tactic same day. No waiting.

---

## Starter picks
- *Atomic Habits* (systems, identity, environment)  
- *The Power of Habit* (cue–routine–reward)  
- *Deep Work* (focus training, distraction control)

[Outro, direct-to-camera]

Reading won’t magically delete bad habits. Reading supplies maps, language, systems—then action turns pages into results.

prompt: give me a research gap  about the Crisis Between Taxis and Ride-Hailing Services in Morocco Rewrite your response. Each section must begin with a thesis statement in italics, use HTML to indicate the italics.
response:
A major research gap is the lack of large-scale, Morocco-specific evidence on how ride-hailing affects taxi drivers’ economic welfare. Most discussion of the taxi–ride-hailing crisis in Morocco relies on anecdotal reporting or limited local observations, but there is still insufficient empirical research measuring changes in taxi drivers’ income, working hours, debt/lease obligations (e.g., license or vehicle costs), job security, and job satisfaction after the entry or attempted entry of ride-hailing platforms. A robust mixed-methods study (quantitative earnings and labor patterns + qualitative interviews on perceived fairness and risk) remains underdeveloped.

A second research gap is the limited assessment of ride-hailing’s real impact on urban mobility outcomes in Moroccan cities. Claims that ride-hailing reduces congestion, improves accessibility, or complements public transport are rarely tested with Moroccan data. Underexplored topics include effects on traffic congestion and vehicle-kilometers traveled, modal shift away from buses/trams, service coverage in peripheral neighborhoods, waiting times, and the extent to which ride-hailing substitutes for or complements existing taxi services in cities such as Casablanca, Rabat, Marrakech, and Tangier.

A third research gap concerns evaluating the effectiveness and fairness of Morocco’s regulatory and governance responses to taxi–platform conflict. Research is still scarce on how existing laws, enforcement practices, and informal arrangements shape competition, safety, pricing, consumer protection, and driver rights across both sectors. Comparative policy analysis—drawing lessons from countries with similar labor markets and licensing systems—could help identify which regulatory models (e.g., licensing reform, platform legalization with conditions, unified safety/insurance standards) best reduce conflict while maintaining service quality and equity.

Overall, the key gap is the absence of integrated, evidence-based research that links driver livelihoods, mobility system performance, and regulation into one coherent Moroccan framework. Most studies treat these issues separately, but the crisis is shaped by their interaction; future research that combines economic data, transport metrics, and policy analysis would better explain the conflict and support practical policy solutions.
