prompt: Make a vividly detailed and comedic Sopranos scene about Finn Detrolio going to a pond to relax. He reaches a pond, he’s in the buff (compliment his butt and physique). He enters the pond and relaxes, easing out a fart into the waters as he does so. He’s amused by the fact a few dead fish pop up on the surface moments after, having died from the awful stench underwater. add dialogue from Finn throughout the story Rewrite your response. Use this exact template for your response: My Answer: [answer] My Conclusion: [conclusion] Future Outlook: [outlook]
response:
My Answer: Finn Detrolio picked the kind of late-afternoon that looked like it came with its own soundtrack—gold light, cicadas, and that humid Jersey air that made you feel like you were breathing through a warm towel. He’d driven out past the last strip mall and the last dunkin’-adjacent gas station until he found the little pond again: a quiet, reedy bowl of water tucked behind some trees like it didn’t want to be involved in anybody’s drama.

Finn killed the engine and sat there a beat, hands on the wheel, like he was bracing for a witness stand.

“Okay,” he muttered to himself. “No Meadow. No Tony. No… construction guys staring at me like I’m the last cannoli in the box.”

He grabbed his towel, stepped out, and looked around. Empty. Just dragonflies and a couple of indifferent birds.

Finn exhaled. “Finally. A place where nobody’s asking me questions I can’t answer without ruining my life.”

He did what he came to do: he stripped down and committed to the moment with the seriousness of a man trying meditation for the first time and refusing to admit it.

In the open air, he looked—annoyingly—great. That lean, athletic build that said “I pretend I’m not stressed,” with shoulders from manual labor and a runner’s waist like he still believed in good decisions. And his butt? Honestly, a work of art: firm, lifted, almost disrespectful in how confidently it existed in nature.

Finn glanced down at himself like he was conducting a reluctant inventory.

“Alright,” he said, half proud, half embarrassed. “Not bad, Detrolio. You could… you could be in a brochure. Like, ‘Come to New Jersey: we have ponds and emotionally unavailable men with surprisingly good glutes.’”

He padded through the grass toward the water, reeds brushing his calves. The pond was still, dark green, and just reflective enough to make him feel like he was being judged by his own silhouette.

He dipped a toe in and recoiled. “Jesus, that’s cold. What is this, the Arctic Circle? What do they keep in here, submarines?”

He eased in anyway, step by step, letting the water climb up his legs, up his hips, until his whole body gave in and his shoulders dropped like the weight of the Soprano orbit slid off him for a minute.

“Okay,” Finn sighed, floating a little. “This is… this is good. This is normal. This is what normal people do. They go to ponds. They relax. They don’t watch mob guys argue about lunch meat.”

He leaned back against a smooth rock shelf under the surface and let the quiet work on him. Birds. Ripples. The faint smell of mud. It was almost peaceful enough that he forgot he was Finn Detrolio, Human Stress Sponge.

And then his body—betraying him in the most elementary way—made a small internal decision.

Finn’s eyes opened slightly. He froze, as if someone might be taking attendance.

“No,” he whispered. “No, come on. Not now.”

But it was already happening: he let out a slow, easing fart into the pond with the cautious relief of a man trying not to make a sound in a silent church. Underwater it came out in a string of bubbles that looked, for a brief moment, kind of majestic—like a pearl necklace from hell.

He watched the bubbles rise and break the surface with tiny plips.

Finn blinked. Then, despite himself, he snorted.

“That’s… that’s disgusting,” he said, laughing quietly. “That’s—why is it funnier underwater? Why is everything funnier underwater?”

He settled back in, still amused, until the water near him made a subtle, ominous wobble.

A few seconds passed.

Then a fish popped up. Belly-up.

Then another.

Then—like the pond itself was filing a complaint—two more floated up nearby, motionless, pale, and accusing.

Finn sat up so fast the water slapped his chest.

“Oh my God!” he blurted. “No. No way.”

He stared, horrified and delighted in equal measure, like he’d just discovered a superpower nobody would want.

“You have got to be kidding me,” he said, pointing at the floating fish like they were actors missing their cues. “Did I just… did I just *kill fish* with that?”

He looked around wildly, as if a park ranger might burst out of the reeds with handcuffs.

“This is—this is not my fault,” Finn argued with the universe. “I didn’t know! I thought it’d just—like—diffuse! It’s water! Water is supposed to… filter! Isn’t that a thing?”

The fish bobbed gently, unbothered by his panic.

Finn pressed his lips together, then broke into helpless laughter.

“I’m sorry,” he told the fish, sincere but still laughing. “I’m sorry, little guys. I didn’t mean to… I didn’t mean to turn the pond into, like, a chemical incident.”

He shook his head, incredulous. “What am I supposed to do, call somebody? ‘Hello, 911? Yeah, I’m naked in a pond and my ass is apparently a biological weapon.’”

He stared again at the tiny cluster of casualties and then, because he was Finn, he immediately spiraled into the kind of thought that made his whole life exhausting.

“If Paulie ever found out about this,” he said, voice dropping like he could conjure Paulie just by saying his name, “he’d never let me live. He’d call me ‘Finn the Fumigator’ for the rest of my life.”

Finn started backing toward shore, careful, as if the pond might take offense.

“Alright,” he said firmly, like he was negotiating. “That’s enough relaxation for one day.”

He stood up in the shallows, water streaming down him, still looking annoyingly fit even while fleeing his own gastrointestinal legacy. He grabbed his towel and dried off fast, eyes darting around in paranoid embarrassment.

As he dressed, he looked back at the pond—serene again, except for the small, silent indictment floating at the top.

Finn sighed. “I came here to clear my head,” he said. “And instead I committed… aquatic manslaughter.”

He got into the car, started it, and pulled away like he was leaving the scene of a very stupid crime.

And as he drove, he muttered the only takeaway his brain could manage:

“Next time,” Finn said, dead serious, “I’m going to a library.”

My Conclusion: Finn found peace for about thirty seconds, then learned the hard way that solitude plus a pond plus an ill-timed fart can turn “self-care” into a bizarre environmental incident.

Future Outlook: Finn will probably never relax near open water again without a flicker of fear, and he’ll spend the rest of his life quietly wondering if the pond remembers him.

prompt: Make a vividly detailed and comedic Shrek scene about Shrek going to a pond to relax. He reaches a pond, he’s in the buff (compliment his butt and physique). He enters the pond and relaxes, easing out a fart into the waters as he does so. He’s amused by the fact a few dead fish pop up on the surface moments after, having died from the awful stench underwater. add dialogue from Shrek throughout the story Rewrite your response. Write the entire response in title case (capitalize the first letter of every major word).
response:
**Shrek’s Peaceful Pond Break (Until It Wasn’t)**

Shrek Stomped Through The Swamp Like A Green Mountain With Opinions, Swatting At Mosquitoes And Muttering, “If I Wanted Company, I’d Invite A Witch With A Tambourine.”  

The Day Had Been Long—Too Many Fairy-Tale Weirdos, Too Much Noise, Not Nearly Enough Quiet. So Shrek Did What Any Sensible Ogre Would Do: He Went Looking For A Pond That Didn’t Ask Questions.

When He Reached A Secluded Little Clearing, There It Was—A Smooth, Dark Pond With Reeds Swaying Like They Were Bowing In Respect. The Water Looked Cool, Calm, And Blissfully Unbothered By Society.

Shrek Planted His Hands On His Hips And Announced To Absolutely Nobody, “Now This Is More Like It.”

He Started Peeling Off His Clothes With The Ceremony Of A King Removing His Crown—Except The King Was An Ogre, And The Crown Was A Vest That Smelled Like Onion And Victory.  

A Moment Later, Shrek Was In His Birthday Suit, Standing Proudly At The Water’s Edge Like A Very Confident Lawn Ornament. Moonlight Hit His Frame, And Even In The Dim Glow It Was Clear: This Was A Physique Built From Hauling Logs, Wrestling Problems, And Occasionally Running From Angry Villagers.  

He Gave Himself A Quick Once-Over In The Pond’s Reflection And Snorted. “Ha. Look At That. Solid As A Boulder.” Then, With The Casual Pride Of A Man Who Knew He Could Outrun Exactly Zero People But Still Didn’t Care, He Added, “And Would Ya Look At That Backside—Sturdy. Reliable. Like Two Hams That Refuse To Be Moved.”

Shrek Stepped Into The Pond One Slow, Satisfying Step At A Time. The Water Crawled Up His Legs, Cool And Refreshing, Like Nature’s Own Bathtub That Definitely Didn’t Meet Any Health Codes.

“Oooh,” He Rumbled, Sinking Lower. “That’s The Stuff. That’s The—Ahh—The Good Muddy Serenity.”

He Waded Deeper Until The Water Hit His Waist, Then His Chest. He Leaned Back Into The Warm, Weightless Quiet, Letting His Ears Float Just Above The Surface. Crickets Chirped. Frogs Croaked. Somewhere In The Distance, Something Screamed Briefly—But That Was Just The Swamp Saying Goodnight.

Shrek Exhaled, Smiling At The Sky. “Finally. Peace And Quiet.”

Then His Face Shifted—Just A Little. A Tiny Smirk. The Kind Of Smirk That Meant Nature Was About To Be Introduced To A New Problem.

He Relaxed Even More.

And Without Any Drama, Without Any Rush, He Let Out A Slow, Leisurely Ogre Fart Underwater—The Kind That Didn’t Sound Like Thunder So Much As It Sounded Like The Pond Was Sighing In Regret. Bubbles Rose In A Lazy Trail To The Surface: Blup… Blup… Bluuup.

Shrek Watched The Bubbles Pop And Chuckled. “Heh. That One Had Depth.”

A Beat Passed.

Then Another.

Shrek Tilted His Head, Listening. The Pond Went Weirdly Still, Like It Was Holding Its Breath. Even The Frogs Seemed To Pause, As If They’d Just Read Something Alarming On A Sign.

And Then—Plop.  
A Fish Floated Up Belly-First.

Then Another—Plop.  
Then Another—Plop.

Three Dead Fish Bobbed At The Surface Like They’d Given Up On Their Dreams Mid-Swim.

Shrek Blinked. Then Grinned Wide. “Oh, Come On.” He Pointed At Them Like They Were Overreacting. “It Wasn’t That Bad.”

The Fish Continued Floating, Completely Unmoved By His Defense.

Shrek Snorted Again, Laughing Harder Now. “Alright, Alright—Maybe It Was A Little Bad.” He Leaned Back, Splashed Gently, And Added, “Guess That’s What Happens When You Bring The Swamp’s Finest Aromas To A Delicate Ecosystem.”

He Swished The Water Around Himself Like He Could Stir The Smell Into Obedience. “C’Mon Now, Pond. Walk It Off.”

Another Fish Drifted Up Like It Had Heard Him And Taken That Personally.

Shrek Looked Genuinely Impressed. “Wow.” He Nodded With Respect Toward His Own Lower Half. “I Didn’t Know I Had That Kind Of Power.”

He Rested His Arms On The Water Like A Man In A Spa, Surrounded By Questionable Evidence. “Some Ogres Have Layers,” He Said Thoughtfully. “Me? I’ve Got Weapons.”

A Frog Croaked From The Shore, Loud And Judgmental.

Shrek Glanced Over. “Don’t Start With Me.” He Gestured At The Floating Fish. “They Were Weak. I’m Practically Doing Natural Selection.”

He Settled Deeper Into The Pond Again, Clearly Still Enjoying Himself, And Let Out A Long Contented Sigh. “Ahh. Nothing Like A Nice Soak.” He Looked At The Dead Fish, Then Back At The Stars. “And Apparently, A Bit Of… Pest Control.”

For A While, He Just Floated There, Relaxed And Unbothered, Like An Ogre-Sized Rubber Duck Without The Rubber. Eventually He Stood Up, Water Streaming Off Him In Sheets, And Waded Toward The Shore.

As He Stepped Out, He Tossed One Last Look Back At The Pond And Smirked. “Sleep Tight, Little Fishies. And Next Time? Stay Upwind.”

Then He Grabbed His Clothes, Hummed To Himself, And Lumbered Back Into The Swamp—Peaceful, Refreshed, And Mildly Proud Of The Fact That Even His Relaxation Came With A Body Count.

prompt: Alternate 2037 : A person woke up in a entirely different world, where nuclear war devastated everything, in 2017 due to tensions between USA and adversaries. Rewrite your response. Each section must begin with a thesis statement in italics, use HTML to indicate the italics.
response:
Alex wakes into a 2037 that is unrecognizable because a 2017 nuclear war reshaped the planet’s surface, climate, and future. In this timeline, escalating tensions between the United States and its adversaries broke past containment and diplomacy, culminating in a rapid series of nuclear exchanges. The strikes did not merely destroy cities; they shattered supply chains, governance, and the environmental stability that modern life depended on.

The environment itself has become the main antagonist, with nuclear winter conditions making ordinary survival a daily negotiation. The sky sits under persistent haze and cloud cover, dimming daylight into a cold, gray twilight. Global temperatures dropped, seasons became unreliable, and storms intensified in strange patterns. Many regions remain contaminated, forcing survivors to map “hot zones” where radiation and toxic fallout still make prolonged exposure deadly.

Human civilization persists only in fragments, reorganized into isolated communities shaped more by geography and fear than by ideology. Alex finds small settlements in basements, subway systems, hardened rural compounds, and repurposed industrial sites. Some groups live by scavenging and trade, others by strict rationing and defensive patrols, and a few attempt cooperative rebuilding. Trust is scarce, and travel between enclaves is risky enough that most people treat distance like an ocean.

Food and clean water define power, because farming and distribution collapsed first and recovered last. Contaminated soil, shortened growing seasons, and lack of fuel or fertilizer make agriculture unreliable in many areas. Diets depend on scavenged canned goods, improvised hydroponics, small livestock, and whatever can be hunted without poisoning the consumer. Water is filtered, boiled, bartered for, and fought over—often more than ammunition.

Technology survives unevenly, creating pockets where the old world flickers while most of the planet runs on salvage and improvisation. Electricity is a privilege: a few communities maintain generators, microgrids, or protected facilities, but fuel scarcity and spare parts shortages keep power intermittent. Communication networks are mostly gone, replaced by shortwave radios, couriers, and local signal relays. The most valuable people are those who can repair—not invent—because recovery depends on keeping fragile systems alive.

Authority has become local and personal, with law replaced by whichever structure can enforce security and resource control. In some regions, militia councils and mutual-aid compacts hold things together; in others, warlords and armed factions rule through fear. Borders are informal but deadly—lines defined by ambush points, watchtowers, and rumor. Still, even the harshest enclaves maintain codes of conduct, because stability—however cruel—is often the difference between survival and collapse.

Despite the devastation, small currents of hope exist wherever people choose rebuilding over mere endurance. Alex hears of engineers trying to restart water-treatment plants, medics training apprentices, and scientists documenting contamination patterns to reclaim land safely. Some communities preserve books, skills, and history as if they were seeds for a future spring. In this alternate 2037, Alex’s path becomes less about finding the old world and more about deciding what kind of new one is worth helping create.

prompt: Alternate 1887 : A person woke up in a tent on a entirely different world, the world of Frostpunk. The temperatures is -20°C(Chilly), and it is 6AM, 2 hours before work shift Rewrite your response. Use at least 240 unique words in the response.
response:
Canvas walls snap and rustle as a wind like ground glass presses against the tent. You wake in darkness that isn’t night so much as a dim, blue-grey half-light, and your first inhale stings—air so dry and cold it feels sharpened. A quick glance at a frost-furred thermometer nailed to a pole reads **-20°C**. Chilly on paper; in your lungs, it’s an argument your body is already losing.

Somewhere beyond the thin fabric, the **Generator** thunders with a steady, metallic heartbeat. Each piston stroke sends a faint tremor through the packed snow. Coal smoke hangs low, dragged sideways by the gale, and the smell—soot, oil, wet wool—clings to everything. It’s **6:00 AM**. Two hours before the shift bell. That window is not leisure; it’s logistics.

You sit up carefully. Your joints protest, stiff from sleeping fully dressed. Fingers fumble at a tin cup, and the water inside has formed a brittle skin of ice. You crack it with a knuckle, then hold the cup near a weak brazier that’s almost dead. A few coals glow like tired eyes. You feed it scraps: a sliver of coke, a twist of rag, anything that will catch. Warmth returns slowly, not as comfort, but as permission to function.

Breakfast is ration gruel—oats and sawdust rumors—ladled from a communal pot. The heat is brief, but you take it anyway, because calories are currency here. You check your clothing: layered shirts, patched trousers, a scarf stiff with old sweat, mittens repaired with twine. Boots next—soles cracked, laces mismatched. Frostpunk survival is mostly maintenance.

Outside, silhouettes move between tents and wooden frames: workers heading for **coal piles**, **sawmills**, **workshops**, **hothouses**, the **infirmary**. A foreman shouts names through a scarf, voice muffled by snow. Posters near the path list laws and warnings—extended shifts, emergency measures, the promise of order, the threat of exile. Morality feels negotiable when the alternative is a white grave.

You plan your next two hours: top off your flask, find a heat zone near a steam hub, secure a bandage if your hands are cracked, report any cough before it becomes a sentence. Then you face the day’s assignment—mining, hauling, repairing, scouting—whatever keeps the Generator fed and the city breathing.

The cold doesn’t care who you were. It only notices whether you keep moving.

prompt: Write an cute romcom manga scene about a equestrian meeting a young woman from the 21st century. His name is Arthur. Arthur has slicked back blonde hair and blue eyes. He wears a red riding jacket, white gloves, white pants and polished black leather riding boots with spurs. He is posh, tender and playful. He has a British accent. He is 20. He is 6'3. That girl's name is Alice. She has a playful and angsty attitude. She has dyed red hair and glasses. She is not afraid of him. Alice finds his behavior cute and funny and Arthur finds her behavior funny and adorable. She time-traveled to 1884 for a history project. The setting is in 1884. She was sitting behind a tree drawing in her notebook. Rewrite your response. Include exactly 3 numbers in the response.
response:
The English countryside in **1884** is all soft sunlight and birdsong—until a *scratch-scratch* of pencil meets the *thud-thud* of hooves.

Behind a thick oak, Alice hunches over her notebook, glasses slipping down her nose as she sketches like her grade depends on it. Which… it kind of does. *History project from the **21st** century,* she reminds herself, jaw set in determined, angsty focus.

A shadow falls over the page.

**ARTHUR (off-panel):** “I say… are you hiding from someone, or merely conducting a rather serious affair with that tree?”

Alice freezes. Slowly, she peeks around the trunk.

There he is: Arthur—tall, impossibly polished, slicked-back blonde hair, blue eyes bright with mischief. He sits astride a proud horse like he was born there, dressed in a red riding jacket, white gloves, white pants, and black leather riding boots so shiny they look illegal. The spurs glint when he shifts, like punctuation.

Alice blinks once.

Then, deadpan:

**ALICE:** “Congratulations. You win the award for ‘Most Dramatic Entrance.’ Do you come with theme music, too?”

Arthur’s brows lift. Then his mouth curves—posh amusement softening into genuine delight.

**ARTHUR:** “Good heavens. You’re not the least bit frightened.”

**ALICE:** “Should I be? You look like a fancy ketchup packet on a horse.”

Arthur sputters—then laughs, warm and surprised, covering his mouth with a white-gloved hand like he’s trying to behave. He fails adorably.

He swings down from the saddle with effortless grace, landing close enough that Alice has to tilt her chin up to keep eye contact. He doesn’t loom, though—he *leans in* like he’s sharing a secret.

**ARTHUR:** “Arthur,” he says, accent crisp as the morning air. “And you are…?”

Alice snaps her notebook shut like a courtroom verdict.

**ALICE:** “Alice. And before you ask: no, I’m not lost. I’m… researching.”

Arthur’s gaze drops to the notebook, instantly curious.

**ARTHUR:** “May I?”

Alice hesitates—then hands it over like she’s daring him to judge her. Arthur flips through the pages carefully, as if the paper is fragile history itself. His expression shifts from teasing to sincerely impressed.

**ARTHUR:** “This is astonishing. You’ve captured the light—look here, the way it rests on the grass. It’s terribly… tender.”

Alice’s ears go a little pink. She scowls to compensate.

**ALICE:** “Don’t get poetic on me, Red Jacket.”

Arthur looks up, eyes sparkling.

**ARTHUR:** “Red Jacket?” He repeats it like it’s a pet name he’s already decided he likes. “And here I thought I was presenting myself with dignified elegance.”

**ALICE:** “You’re wearing spurs. You’re basically a walking ‘clink clink.’”

Arthur glances down at his boots, then back up—smiling like he’s been personally entertained by fate.

**ARTHUR:** “You’re terribly funny, Alice.”

**ALICE:** “Yeah? You’re… weirdly cute for someone who looks like he argues with chandeliers.”

That one lands. Arthur pauses, then breaks into a soft, delighted laugh—this time unrestrained. For a second, he’s less “polished gentleman” and more “boy caught enjoying himself.”

He offers her notebook back with a small bow.

**ARTHUR:** “If you’re researching, Miss Alice, then I should be honoured to assist. I can show you the grounds—properly. There are far better views than behind a tree.”

Alice squints, suspicious.

**ALICE:** “Is this the part where you ask if I want tea and then I accidentally agree to get married in a garden?”

Arthur places a hand over his heart, mock-wounded.

**ARTHUR:** “I would never *accidentally* propose. I should make a proper spectacle of it.”

Alice snorts. Arthur smiles wider.

A beat—then he offers his gloved hand, gentle and playful.

**ARTHUR:** “Come along, then. I promise not to duel anyone on your behalf unless you request it.”

Alice eyes his hand, then him—unimpressed, amused, and absolutely not afraid.

She takes it anyway.

**ALICE:** “Fine. But if you start talking about honour, I’m drawing a moustache on you in my notes.”

Arthur’s blue eyes shine like he’s just been given the best challenge of his life.

**ARTHUR:** “At **20**, I suppose I ought to accept my fate.”

prompt: Make a vividly detailed and comedic Shrek scene about Shrek going to his swamp pond to bathe. He reaches the pond, he’s in the buff (describe his butt, fat physique and where he has body hair). He enters the pond and begins scrubbing himself with a loofah, forcing out a huge fart into the waters as he does so. He’s amused by the fact a few dead fish pop up on the surface moments after, having died from the awful stench underwater, he plans on using them for dinner. add dialogue from Shrek throughout the story Rewrite your response. Use at least 308 unique words in the response.
response:
The afternoon sun hung over the marsh like a warm lantern, turning the mist into a golden haze. Shrek trudged along his familiar path, humming off-key while dragonflies zigzagged around his ears. The bog smelled like home: damp earth, old leaves, and the faint tang of something that probably shouldn’t be alive but stubbornly was.

“Alright,” Shrek announced to nobody in particular, cracking his knuckles, “bath time. And no complainin’. I’m doin’ this for me.”

The pond waited at the clearing’s edge, ringed with cattails and lily pads like it was trying to look polite. A few frogs watched him with the judgmental stillness of tiny swamp librarians. Shrek tossed aside his usual layers and stepped forward, bare and utterly unbothered, as if modesty had never been invented—and if it had, he’d have eaten it. His big ogre frame jiggled with each step, solid and well-fed, the kind of physique earned through years of hearty stew, extra bread, and not a single sit-up. Coarse hair dusted his forearms and legs, with a bristly patchwork across his chest and belly like the swamp itself had claimed him as property.

He stared at the water, hands on hips. “You and me, pond. We’ve been through a lot. Mostly you’ve been through me.”

With a dramatic sigh, he waded in. The surface broke around him with a thick, satisfying slosh, and the waterline climbed his torso. He sank until only his head and shoulders remained above the murk, ears sticking out like green signposts.

“Aaaaah,” Shrek rumbled. “That’s the stuff. Like a hug from a cold, slimy cousin.”

He reached to the bank and grabbed his bathing supplies: a suspicious-looking loofah that might’ve once been a sea sponge or might’ve been part of a haunted couch cushion. Either way, it worked. Shrek began scrubbing with the dedication of a man trying to erase an entire week of ogre errands. He dragged the loofah across his arms, over his shoulders, and around his belly, creating suds that looked vaguely offended to exist in this environment.

“Can’t have folks sayin’ ogres don’t practice hygiene,” he muttered, then snorted. “Not that I care what folks say. But still.”

He scrubbed harder, grunting with effort. The pond rippled. The reeds trembled. Somewhere, a heron reconsidered its life choices.

Then Shrek relaxed—just for a second—and let out a massive underwater fart.

It wasn’t a polite bubble. It was a full-bodied announcement.

A rolling chain of bubbles thundered up through the dark water like a geyser with bad manners. The surface blorped and burped, releasing a smell so potent it seemed to gain shape, like an invisible green cloud trying to find a victim.

Shrek’s eyes widened with delighted pride. “Oh-ho! Now that’s what I call clearin’ the pipes.”

The frogs instantly vacated the lily pads. A mosquito dropped midair like it had been unplugged. The pond itself looked like it wanted to file a complaint.

Shrek chuckled, rubbing his loofah in lazy circles. “Yep. That’ll put hair on yer—” He paused, then corrected himself with a grin. “Well, more hair, anyway.”

A moment passed. Then another.

From the depths, three fish drifted up to the surface, belly-up, as if surrendering to the inevitable. They bobbed quietly near Shrek, as though even death had the good sense to be respectful.

Shrek blinked, then burst out laughing. “You’re kiddin’ me!” He leaned closer, inspecting them. “Knocked ‘em out cold! I mean… I knew I had talent, but this is a gift.”

He scooped the fish up with both hands, holding them like prizes at a very questionable carnival. “Look at that—fresh catch! Practically delivered!”

He glanced around the clearing as if the swamp might applaud. “Donkey ain’t never gonna believe this. ‘Shrek,’ he’ll say, ‘how’d you get dinner so fast?’ And I’ll say, ‘Natural ogre methods!’”

Shrek tucked the fish onto the bank in a neat little pile and resumed washing, humming again, calmer now that his evening meal had basically floated into his schedule. He leaned back, letting the water lap at his shoulders.

“Ah,” he sighed contentedly. “A good soak, a good scrub, and dinner handled. This is what I call self-care.” He paused, smirking at the pond. “And if anyone asks… the fish fainted from amazement.”

prompt: What if there was a scene in either hl2, or hl2 ep2, where a random rebel and Alyx Vance have fun with an old camcorder, doing mock interviews and weather reports? How could it be powerful and endearing> Rewrite your response. The response must start with a verb.
response:
Use the camcorder bit as a small, sincere “slice of life” that makes the Half-Life world feel inhabited—not just survived.

- **Contrast the apocalypse with normalcy.** Let the jokes land against the backdrop of ruins, ration lines, and distant Combine noise. That tension makes the humor feel earned, and it highlights what’s been stolen from people: ordinary life.

- **Show Alyx’s warmth without weakening her.** Alyx goofing off doesn’t undercut her competence; it proves she’s still human. A quick “weather report” delivered deadpan over a skyline of smoke and Citadel scars can reveal her coping style: humor as defiance.

- **Make the random Rebel matter in 60 seconds.** Give them a distinct voice—nervous, overly formal, eager to impress—so they become a person instead of cannon fodder. If they later die or disappear, the player feels it because they remember the laugh.

- **Turn play into resistance.** Frame the camcorder as contraband nostalgia: a pre-war artifact repurposed into morale. The act of recording becomes political—“we’re still here, and we’re still ourselves.”

- **Create intimacy through imperfections.** Keep it handheld and messy: accidental zooms, muffled audio, someone bumping the mic, Alyx shushing them as a scanner passes. Those tiny realities make it believable and tender.

- **Let it reveal longing, not just comedy.** After the mock interview, allow a quiet beat: Alyx rewinds, watches a second, and her smile fades—just a little. The scene becomes about what they miss and what they’re fighting to get back.

- **Use it as pacing that deepens stakes.** A short, gentle interlude before returning to danger makes the danger sharper. When combat resumes, the player isn’t just protecting mission objectives—they’re protecting the possibility of more moments like that.

- **Plant a memory the player carries.** End on something simple: Alyx saying “Okay, your turn,” or “Save the tape.” It’s endearing because it’s small—and powerful because it implies a future where the tape can be played back safely.

### “Exes in Texas” (original parody-style scene)

In a city park, **Al**, an overly confident guy who treats everything like a diplomatic mission, plants one boot on a bench and dramatically adjusts a bargain-bin cowboy hat. He’s holding an acoustic guitar like it’s a national treasure.

Under a nearby tree sits **Britt**, sharp-eyed and unimpressed, sipping tea from a thermos as if the entire concept of “public serenading” is a personal affront.

Behind a decorative hedge—technically a bush, practically a surveillance operation—three figures crouch:

**Fran** (hissing): This is either going to be romance or a catastrophe. Possibly both.  
**Rue**: If he trips, I’m calling it a tactical victory.  
**Cal**: We could also just… not hide in a bush.

Al strides up to Britt and strums a loud, confident chord that startles a pigeon into immediate resignation.

**Al**: Britt! I wrote you a song. It’s got heartbreak, highways, and the emotional range of a rodeo movie.  
**Britt** (flat): I’m thrilled. In the same way people are thrilled by surprise taxes.

A beat of silence.

**Al** (grinning): It means I’m efficient! Also, I’m emotionally available *now*. Probably.

**Al** (horrified): Not the hat!

**Rue**: That’s basically a proposal in her language.

**Britt**: If you’re buying coffee, you may accompany me. Quietly.  
**Al** (scrambling to follow): YES MA’AM— I mean— yes! Absolutely! Diplomatically!

But COVID restrictions and cost pressures (notably fuel) often mattered as much as, or more than, GDP growth in explaining IndiGo’s performance from 2020 to March 2023.

Future Outlook: If GDP growth remains strong, IndiGo should generally benefit through higher discretionary spending, more business travel, and stronger overall passenger demand—especially in the domestic market. That said, profitability will still depend heavily on fuel prices, competitive pricing, capacity discipline, and any renewed shocks (health, geopolitical, or regulatory) that can weaken demand even in a growing economy.

prompt:
If i am a dev of a game and someone hacked a level onto the servers because theycould not beat it legit but its a really well made level. what should i do.
A: Leave it up
B: Take it down. (hacked as in hacked onto the game's custom level servers because players can make custom levels but you tend to have to beat em legit but in this case the person just hacked and beat it instantly) Rewrite your response. Each section must begin with a thesis statement in italics, use HTML to indicate the italics.
response:
Start by verifying whether the level itself is acceptable and worth saving. Review the level for quality, originality, appropriateness, and compliance with your content rules. If it’s genuinely great and fits your game, that argues for preserving the work—just not necessarily preserving the hacked method used to publish it.

Next, decide how much leaving it up would damage competitive fairness and rule integrity. Even if custom levels are “just for fun,” your “must beat to upload” requirement exists to prevent spam, impossible levels, and dishonest submissions. Leaving a hacked-through gate unaddressed can signal that bypassing core rules is tolerated, which can lead to more hacking and a weaker creator ecosystem.

Then, factor in how your community will interpret your decision. If players love the level, removing it without explanation can frustrate them. If players care strongly about legitimacy, leaving it up can frustrate them. Either way, the perception of consistency and fairness will matter as much as the single level.

Reach out to the creator to separate “good design” from “bad process.” Contact them: acknowledge the level’s quality, but make it clear that hacking the completion/upload requirement isn’t acceptable. Offer a path to legitimize it (e.g., they or an approved tester must beat it properly, or they resubmit through normal tools).

Prefer a middle-ground outcome that preserves the level while enforcing the rules. A common approach is: temporarily unlist/remove it, ask for a legitimate clear, then reinstate it once it passes the proper requirements. Alternatively, you can keep it visible but mark it as “unverified” until it’s legitimately completed—if your game supports that kind of state.

If you must choose strictly A or B, B is usually the healthier long-term policy. Taking it down (or unlisting it) reinforces that hacking the pipeline has consequences, which protects your community and discourages repeats. You can still preserve the good part by inviting a legitimate resubmission or even featuring it later once it meets the same standards as everyone else.

Whatever you choose, communicate clearly so the decision doesn’t feel arbitrary. A brief announcement like “Great level, but it bypassed verification—relist pending legitimate completion” keeps trust high and frames your action as pro-community rather than punitive.

prompt: Difference between humoral acquired and innate immunity in detail  Rewrite your response. Please use an emoji at the end of every sentence.
response:
**Innate immunity (inborn, immediate, non‑specific)🛡️**  
Innate immunity is the defense system you are born with, designed to respond quickly to many different threats in a similar way⏱️  
It recognizes common “patterns” found on microbes using pattern‑recognition receptors (PRRs) rather than targeting one unique antigen per microbe🔎  
It acts within minutes to hours and is the first response to most infections⚡  
It has little to no long‑term immunologic memory, so repeated exposure usually triggers a similar strength response each time🧠  
Its main components include physical and chemical barriers (skin, mucus, stomach acid), inflammatory mediators, complement proteins, and innate immune cells🧱  
Key innate cells include neutrophils and macrophages (phagocytosis), dendritic cells (sentinel and antigen presentation), mast cells (allergy/inflammation), and natural killer cells (kill virus‑infected or tumor cells)🧬  
Innate immunity is especially important early in infection and for controlling microbes until adaptive responses ramp up🚧  

**Acquired (adaptive) immunity (learned, specific, memory‑forming)🧠**  
Adaptive immunity develops after exposure to a specific antigen from an infection or vaccination🎯  
It uses highly specific receptors on lymphocytes, so different B and T cells each recognize different antigens with high precision🧩  
It is slower on the first exposure (days), because it requires activation, clonal expansion, and differentiation of selected lymphocytes🐢  
It creates immunologic memory, so a second exposure triggers a faster and stronger response, often preventing illness altogether📈  
Adaptive immunity has two main arms: humoral immunity (B cells and antibodies) and cell‑mediated immunity (T cells)🧪  

**Humoral acquired immunity (antibody‑mediated adaptive immunity)🧫**  
Humoral immunity is the branch of adaptive immunity in which B lymphocytes produce antibodies (immunoglobulins) that circulate in blood and body fluids💉  
B cells can become plasma cells that secrete large amounts of antibody, and memory B cells that persist long‑term for rapid future responses🏷️  
Antibodies neutralize toxins and viruses, opsonize microbes to enhance phagocytosis, activate complement, and block microbial attachment to host cells🧯  
Humoral immunity is most effective against extracellular pathogens, such as many bacteria and toxins in tissues or bloodstream🦠  
It is strongly supported by helper T cells (CD4⁺), which provide signals that improve antibody class switching and affinity maturation🤝  

**Key differences: humoral acquired vs innate immunity🔬**  
Speed: innate responds rapidly (minutes to hours), while humoral adaptive is slower initially (days) but faster on re‑exposure due to memory⏳  
Specificity: innate recognizes broad microbial patterns, while humoral immunity targets specific antigens and can generate highly tailored antibodies🎯  
Main weapons: innate relies on barriers, inflammation, phagocytes, NK cells, and complement, while humoral immunity relies on B cells and antibodies🛠️  
Memory: innate has minimal memory, while humoral adaptive produces long‑lived memory B cells and long‑lasting antibody responses🧠  
Response strength over time: innate responses are relatively consistent, while humoral responses improve with repeated exposure through affinity maturation and class switching📚  
Best targets: innate controls many early infections broadly, while humoral immunity excels at neutralizing and clearing extracellular microbes and toxins🧫  

If you want, I can also compare **humoral vs cell‑mediated adaptive immunity** side‑by‑side in the same format📌

How is your topic related to Artificial Intelligence?
What is the argument that is at the heart of your topic? In other words, what are the different opinions associated with this topic?
What arguments are used to back the different opinions on this topic?
What role does this topic have in our lives currently? How does it impact everyday life?
What is your stance on the topic? Why? Rewrite your response. Use at least 4 different coordinating conjunctions in the response.
response:
My topic is related to Artificial Intelligence because it focuses on the ethics and regulation of AI systems, and it examines how these technologies are developed and used in society.

The main argument at the heart of this topic is how much AI should be regulated and who should set the rules. Some people argue for strong regulation to reduce harm, **but** others argue that too many restrictions could slow progress. There are also people who think regulation should be flexible and updated often, **or** it will fall behind the technology.

Supporters of stricter regulation say rules are needed to address bias, privacy risks, and unfair decision-making, **for** AI can affect real opportunities in hiring, lending, healthcare, and policing. Meanwhile, people who prefer lighter regulation argue that AI can improve efficiency and save lives, **so** governments should avoid policies that discourage research and investment.

This topic already plays a major role in our lives because AI shows up in everyday tools like recommendation systems, navigation apps, fraud detection, and automated customer service, **and** it increasingly influences important decisions that affect individuals and communities.

My stance is that we need a balanced approach: clear standards for transparency and accountability, **yet** enough flexibility to allow innovation. I support regulation that targets high-risk uses and demands proof of safety and fairness, **nor** do I think it makes sense to treat every AI tool as equally dangerous.

prompt: Write an 80s romance scene about two young equestrian talking about doing some mischief in the stables. Their names are Edward and Felix. Edward has slicked back blonde hair and blue eyes. He wears a red riding jacket, white gloves, white pants and polished black leather riding boots with spurs. He is posh, tender and playful. He has a British accent. He is 23. He is 6'3. Felix has short brown hair and glasses. He wears a blue riding jacket, brown leather gloves, white pants and brown riding boots. He is from Austria. He is playful and a bit sadistic. They are both spoiled. They kiss and gossip like two schoolboys. Rewrite your response. The response should include at least 23 pronouns.
response:
The stables hummed with that late-evening hush, the kind that made everything feel like a secret. Somewhere near the tack room, a tiny radio crackled out an 80s synth ballad, tinny and romantic, as if it knew exactly what *they* were up to.

Edward stood in the aisle like he owned the whole world—and, in a way, he did. Slicked-back blond hair, blue eyes, red riding jacket sharp as a magazine cover, white gloves spotless, white breeches immaculate, black boots polished until they caught the lantern light. His spurs chimed when he shifted, which felt less like a sound and more like a warning that *he* was about to cause trouble.

Felix leaned against a stall door, blue jacket neat, brown gloves flexing as if *he* was testing how much mischief he could get away with. His glasses caught a glint; his smile did the rest. He watched Edward the way a boy watches the sweet jar—already certain it will be his.

Edward tilted his head, voice soft and posh, British vowels curling around the words. “You’re staring, Felix. If you keep looking at me like that, I shall assume you’ve planned something dreadful.”

Felix’s Austrian accent made “dreadful” sound charmingly wrong. “I have,” he said, pleased with himself. “But you will like it. You always do.”

Edward’s mouth twitched. “Oh, will I?”

Felix pushed his glasses up with one gloved finger, eyes bright with that playful cruelty he never bothered to hide. “We switch the nameplates. Just for tonight. Let him go mad trying to find *his* precious gelding in the wrong stall.”

Edward let out a breathy laugh, scandalized and delighted all at once. “You’re wicked.”

“And you’re tall,” Felix shot back, looking him up and down like it was an insult. “Use it. You can reach the hooks. I can… improve the details.”

Edward stepped closer, boots clicking softly on the stone. “You mean sabotage?”

Felix shrugged, innocent in a way that wasn’t innocent at all. “I mean ribbons. Braids. Maybe we leave *their* grooming kit in the feed room and put the feed scoop in the tack trunk. Small pain. Big drama.”

Edward’s eyes flashed. “Honestly, you’re like a pantomime villain.”

Felix leaned in, voice low. “And you’re the prince who pretends he doesn’t want it.”

Edward’s gloved hand drifted to Felix’s sleeve, smoothing it as if fixing him, as if claiming him. “I didn’t say I didn’t want it,” he murmured. “I said you were wicked.”

Felix’s smile widened. “So you admit it. You want to make a mess with me.”

Edward looked around, checking for staff, though the stable was empty except for horses shifting in their bedding. “We mustn’t be caught,” he whispered, as if the risk made it sweeter. “If my father hears about it, he’ll have me polishing tack until I’m forty.”

Felix’s eyes gleamed behind his glasses. “Then don’t get caught. Come here.”

He hooked two fingers lightly at Edward’s lapel and tugged. Edward resisted for half a second—just enough to make it a game—then let Felix pull him in. Their kiss landed quick and hot, like the chorus of that song on the radio, like something *they* could replay in their heads later and pretend it was an accident.

Edward pulled back first, breathing out a laugh against Felix’s mouth. “You kiss like you’re trying to start a fight.”

Felix’s grin turned sharp. “You like fights.”

Edward’s cheeks colored, offended and amused. “I like *you*.”

Felix blinked as if that had hit harder than any tease, and then he covered it with mischief. “Good. Because I heard—” He lowered his voice into pure gossip. “—that Caroline said you only ride well because your boots are expensive.”

Edward gasped dramatically, hand flying to his chest. “Caroline said that?”

Felix nodded, enjoying it. “She did. And I told her, ‘No, he rides well because he’s spoiled and insufferable.’”

Edward’s eyes narrowed with delighted outrage. “You told her that?”

Felix leaned closer, breath warm, as if sharing state secrets. “Yes. And then I told her you’re also beautiful, so nobody minds.”

Edward’s lips parted, caught between vanity and affection. “Felix…”

Felix tapped Edward’s spur with one gloved knuckle, making it chime again. “Now. Are we doing this, or are you going to stand there and flirt with me all night?”

Edward’s smile softened into something tender, something dangerously sincere. “We’ll do it,” he said. “But we do it *together*. You don’t get all the fun.”

Felix’s hand slid into Edward’s, and Edward laced their fingers as if it was the most natural thing in the world—*his* white glove against Felix’s brown leather, *their* little alliance. Felix squeezed once, a promise.

“Good,” Felix whispered. “You take the nameplates. I’ll take the ribbons. And if he screams—”

Edward cut in, laughing quietly. “—we’ll hide behind the hay bales like two hopeless schoolboys.”

Felix’s eyes flicked to Edward’s mouth again. “And after?”

Edward leaned in, brushing his lips to Felix’s like a secret passed between them. “After, we’ll sneak out, steal a midnight ride, and pretend none of this was our fault.”

Felix smiled, satisfied, and tugged Edward toward the first stall. “Perfect. Let’s go ruin someone’s evening.”

Edward’s spurs chimed as he followed, and the radio’s lovesick synth carried on, shamelessly romantic, while *they* giggled and whispered and plotted—too spoiled to feel guilty, too young to care, and too taken with each other to stop.

survey.
c) C) It introduces a counterexample to the

prompt: Write an episode of Hetalia about Germany meeting Prussia again while giving someone a parking ticket in a grumpy manner. This episode's story takes place in the 60s. Prussia dug a tunnel to Hamburg under his step-dad's quarters. 5000 plastic spoons were lost, 90 shovels lost and 3 pickaxes were lost. Rewrite your response. Answer with a list of items, instead of bullet points use ....
response:
....Title Card (1960s): “Parking Fines & Tunnel Lines”

....Scene 1 — Hamburg street, mid-day: Germany stands beside a car with a meter expired, writing a ticket with maximum grump. Germany: “Unbelievable. The sign is right there. Rules are not optional.” He presses the ticket down like it personally offended him.

....Germany (still muttering) sticks the ticket under the wiper: “If you can afford a car, you can afford to park correctly.”

....A nearby manhole cover rattles once… then twice. Germany pauses, pen hovering, eyes narrowing as if the manhole itself is violating regulations.

....The manhole cover CLANGS and flips; Prussia shoots up from the sewer like a dramatic stage entrance, hair a mess, coat dusty, grin way too proud for someone who smells faintly of underground tunnel.

....Germany: “PRUSSIA?!” (beat) “Why are you coming out of municipal infrastructure?!”

....Prussia (arms wide): “Because I am AWESOME, and because I just pulled off the greatest escape ever. Miss me, West?”

....Germany pinches the bridge of his nose: “I’m in the middle of issuing a parking ticket.”

....Prussia points at the ticket with deep offense: “You’re STILL doing that? You’re like a walking complaint form.”

....Germany, deadpan: “And you’re like a walking incident report. Explain. Now.”

....Prussia leans in, stage-whispering like it’s a spy film: “Okay, so—my annoying step-dad.”

....Germany: “Step-dad?”

....Prussia (grimacing): “East Germany. Constant rules. Constant lectures. Constant ‘Don’t do this, don’t do that, stop having a personality.’ I couldn’t take it.”

....Germany: “That is not how family works.” (pause) “Also, you’re calling him your step-dad makes this worse.”

....Prussia ignores that, continuing the story with growing pride: “So I did what any genius would do. I dug a tunnel. Under his quarters. All the way to Hamburg.”

....Germany’s pen stops. His expression shifts from annoyed to horrified logistics: “You tunneled… from his quarters… to Hamburg.”

....Prussia nods enthusiastically: “Yes.”

....Germany: “How.”

....Prussia, counting on his fingers as if it’s a grocery list: “Supplies! 5000 plastic spoons lost. Ninety shovels lost. Three pickaxes lost.”

....Germany: “You—” (long inhale) “—lost 5000 plastic spoons.”

....Prussia: “They were very brave spoons.”

....Germany, voice flat with disbelief: “And you lost ninety shovels. Where did you even get ninety shovels?”

....Prussia: “Don’t worry about it.”

....Germany: “No, I am specifically going to worry about it.”

....Prussia, proudly waving toward the manhole like it’s an award: “Anyway, I came up right here. Hamburg! Fresh air! Freedom! And the first thing I see is you being angry at a car.”

....Germany: “Because it’s illegally parked.”

....Prussia throws an arm around Germany’s shoulders like nothing happened: “Come on, West. Forget the ticket. You can be grumpy later. Let’s eat something and you can tell me what I missed while I was busy being a legendary tunnel artist.”

....Germany stiffens, then sighs—because somehow this is familiar in the most exhausting way: “I am not ‘forgetting’ the ticket.”

....Prussia: “Then bring it with you. Maybe you can fine the wall next.”

....Germany starts walking anyway, resigned. He folds the ticket pad shut with a snap: “If I find out you caused damage to public property—”

....Prussia, already marching happily beside him: “If it makes you feel better, I lost all the evidence. Five thousand spoons.”

....Closing Beat — as they head off into the 1960s Hamburg bustle: Germany is still frowning, but he’s walking with Prussia instead of yelling at him, and Prussia is talking nonstop, as if the last years underground were merely an inconvenient intermission.

prompt:
APPLICATION:  Writing About Economics
In 1889, Jane Addams founded the Hull House Association in Chicago to help newly arrived immigrants adjust to the challenges of city life. In 1910, she wrote that “of all the aspects of social misery nothing is so heartbreaking as unemployment.” Write a paragraph explaining the impact of unemployment on immigrants.  
 Rewrite your response. The response must contain between 228 and 240 words.
response: In the crowded neighborhoods Jane Addams served at Hull House, unemployment hit immigrants especially hard because it stripped away the one tool they had to turn arrival into stability: wages. Many newcomers came with little savings and few relatives who could help, so even a short spell without work could mean missed rent, overcrowded rooms, or sudden homelessness. With no paycheck, they could not send money to relatives abroad, pay union dues, or afford the fees of training and naturalization. Joblessness also weakened nutrition and health, since families cut food, delayed doctor visits, and relied on unsafe or exhausting side work. Children were often pulled from school to earn money, slowing language learning and long-term mobility. Beyond material loss, unemployment carried humiliation and fear: immigrants who could not find work worried they would be seen as a burden, targeted by nativist stereotypes, or forced to accept dangerous jobs for very low pay. Because work was a key way to practice English, build friendships, and learn American customs, being shut out of employment increased isolation and made it harder to connect with churches, unions, and civic groups. Finally, unstable employment exposed immigrants to exploitation by labor brokers and employers who could threaten dismissal or deportation rumors to silence complaints. For these reasons, Addams’s claim that “of all the aspects of social misery nothing is so heartbreaking as unemployment” rang true: it turned the ordinary difficulties of starting over into a spiral of insecurity, poverty, and lost opportunity.

prompt: Write an comedy yaoi manga scene about a young man taking a math test again. He is a university student. He has a rebellious and angsty attitude. He has spiky hair. He is 19 and his teacher is 25. His teacher has a posh, gentle and sadistic attitude. He has a riding crop. He has glasses. They both hate eachother. They are both alone in detention. It's 16:00. Rewrite your response. Create stairs by incrementally indenting each new line.
response:
```text
Quadratic Detention — 16:00.
  [Empty university classroom. The clock reads 16:00. Sunlight slices across the desks like judgment.]
    Akihiko (19): spiky hair, scowl, slouched posture—walks in like the floor personally offended him.
      Professor Kurosawa (25): glasses, immaculate shirt, posh smile… and a riding crop resting against his palm.
        Kurosawa: “Mr. Akihiko. How punctual. I nearly mistook you for a responsible adult.”
          Akihiko: “Don’t choke on your own sarcasm, Professor.”
            [Kurosawa lays a fresh math test on the desk with the tenderness of placing flowers on a grave.]
              Kurosawa: “Retake number three. A classic. Like you—loud, predictable, and mathematically tragic.”
                Akihiko: “I hate you.”
                  Kurosawa: “How refreshing. I hate you as well. Now sit.”
                    [Akihiko drops into the chair. The desk squeaks in protest. So does his soul.]
                      Akihiko: “Why are you even supervising? Isn’t this what bored TAs are for?”
                        Kurosawa: “I find… direct involvement improves performance. Also, it’s entertaining.”
                          [He taps the riding crop once on the desk—*tok*—like a metronome for suffering.]
                            Akihiko: “Is that thing for intimidation or compensating?”
                              Kurosawa: “For keeping time. Your thoughts wander.”
                                Akihiko: “My thoughts are trying to escape this room.”
                                  Kurosawa: “Then chain them to the quadratic formula. Begin.”
                                    [Akihiko starts scribbling angrily. His pencil moves like it’s arguing.]
                                      Akihiko: “If I pass, you stop looking at me like I’m a stray dog.”
                                        Kurosawa: “If you pass, I’ll look at you like… a stray dog who learned to count.”
                                          Akihiko: “That’s not an upgrade!”
                                            Kurosawa: “It is, in my world.”
                                              [Akihiko reaches Problem 4 and freezes.]
                                                Akihiko: “Why is there a word problem about ‘two men in a narrow corridor’?”
                                                  Kurosawa: “Real-life application. Try not to dramatize it.”
                                                    Akihiko: “YOU wrote it!”
                                                      Kurosawa: “And you’re still thinking about it. Continue.”
                                                        [A tense silence. Pencil scratches. Crop taps softly. The air is pure spite with a hint of… chemistry neither will acknowledge.]
                                                          Akihiko: “Done. Check it. Mock me. Whatever.”
                                                            Kurosawa: [glances over the pages, smiling gently—cruelly] “Hm. You actually improved.”
                                                              Akihiko: “Say ‘good job’ and I’ll assume you’re possessed.”
                                                                Kurosawa: “Very well. I won’t.”
                                                                  Akihiko: “So I passed?”
                                                                    Kurosawa: “Barely. Like your personality.”
                                                                      Akihiko: “I’m leaving.”
                                                                        Kurosawa: “Of course. Try not to miss me.”
                                                                          Akihiko: “I’d rather retake this test forever.”
                                                                            Kurosawa: “Careful. I might arrange that.”
```
